subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be back in an old home of mine. This is where I belong.
First, sir, I would like to commend and congratulate you as Deputy Speaker and as Chairman of the Committee of the Whole. 1 commend and congratulate also the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) for the excellent presentations they made on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I am indeed fortunate in being able to represent Hamilton Mountain. I say this with all sincerity because I was the recipient of only 42 per cent of the popular vote. But I will tell this House and my constituents in Hamilton Mountain that I will be constant in my duties and do the best I can for the benefit of Canada in general and my constituents in particular.
As I mentioned earlier, this is not a new experience for me. I was here before, in the Twenty-ninth Parliament. However, this time I sit on the right side of the House, so it is a new experience for me in that regard.
I suppose Hamilton Mountain could be termed, in political terms at least, a swing riding, but I do not see why that should mitigate against my doing a responsible job. On the contrary, I
October 11, 1979

think it makes us all the more cognizant of the mood of the peoole of our ridings and of Canadians in general.
From Mountain Lookout the visitor enjoys a scenic panorama with miles of residential and commercial development in the foreground. In the middle distance is the heavy industry of Canada, the third most important manufacturing city and the home of Canada's two largest steel mills, the whole framed by the dramatic and exciting Burlington Skyway in the background. Front and centre in Canada's golden horseshoe area, Hamilton sits at the strategic west end of Lake Ontario.
It is indeed an idyllic setting for a city. But the natural beauty also gives the city a number of geographical advantages. The advantages of location, harbour and the escarpment would shape Hamilton's commercial and industrial future. It is located at the junction of two great waterways, the United States Mohawk-Hudson and Canada's first inland highway, the St. Lawrence River.
Hamilton Bay is an ideal harbour. It is protected by a sand bar sheltering it from the rougher waters of Lake Ontario. This protective harbour saved the British Navy and perhaps Canada from the Americans during the War of 1812 when the navy slipped into the harbour. Some suggest we have a navy in Canada which is disappearing. I am sure our government will be doing something about that.
The escarpment on the mountain itself has been an asset. It was formed by glacial deposits on the receding of the ice age. The sedimentary rock of shale, sandstone and particularly limestone provided necessary raw materials for industry. With all these natural assets one might say that a city at the end of Lake Ontario was inevitable, but one would not have predicted a city with the vibrancy and diversity of Hamilton today. These geographical advantages were used by past generations of Hamiltonians to make it Canada's industrial giant, as well as the second largest city in Ontario, producing 60 per cent of the nation's steel, which in turn is responsible for Hamilton being the third largest port in terms of tonnage in Canada.
It is against such an economic backdrop that Canada's two largest steelmakers, the Steel Company of Canada and Dominion Foundries, are pushing ahead with significant increases in capacity. In 1978, Dofasco brought into production its new steel-making shop which represented at that time the largest single capital investment in that company's history. But this project, important as it was to Hamilton and to Canada, was dwarfed in an announcement by the company last week of a new mill, the construction of which is to cost $350 million. And just six months from now, Stelco will pour the first steel at its Lake Erie development, in an expansion program which is the largest single venture in the history of the Canadian steel industry. So even in these times of economic troubles I am proud to say that Hamilton, the ambitious city, is holding its own.
There were, however, problems with respect to getting help from federal governments in the past; hopefully, there will not be the same difficulty in the future. There is, for example, the
The Address-Mr. Beattie
question of seaway tolls so central to keeping these giants of industry expanding and keeping Canadians working. I might refer to the blatant discrimination of seaway tolls as they pertain to bulk cargo vis-a-vis general cargo. There is also the matter of a commitment made by the previous government- nothing final has yet been determined-concerning funding for an important expansion project in Hamilton harbour.
We also have an airport, of a sort, in Hamilton whose
215,000	movements a year-215,000 movements, yes-placed it seventh in the whole of Canada, ahead of Mirabel, Windsor and Winnipeg, just to mention a few. The city of Hamilton has been clamouring for the last ten years for expanded facilities, improved runways, better lighting and navigational aids. In 1973, as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, I asked a question regarding the expansion of Hamilton airport and was told a decision would be made after the completion of environmental studies. Mr. Speaker, six years later I find they are still studying the environment. At this point we know the habitat of every bullfrog and reed in Wentworth county but still no decision has been reached. Can anyone question the attitude of some Hamiltonians who claim they work hard all year and ask where it gets them in terms of promises from government? To copy a well-known television advertisement, they get it in the back, the neck and God knows where else. Am I asking too much when I press at this point for a decision which would eliminate the atmosphere of uncertainty surrounding this extremely important project? I think not.
Hamilton, I might add, is a city destined to grow and prosper, an ambitious city. It might well be termed a city within a city, because as is the trend in most metropolitan areas many workers live in the suburbs and commute to work. Today, 30 per cent of the population live atop the escarpment, hence the term "split level city" and the name "Hamilton Mountain" for the constituency which I proudly represent. So part of the area could be described as a bedroom community for the city proper and is highly cosmopolitan, its population made up of many ethnic groups. These new Canadians, through their activities and by reason of their heritage, add colour and depth to the city's cultural fabric which does much to build a sense of co-operation and understanding among all the citizens. Hamilton is a richer community as a result and is a microcosm of Canada in this regard.
I am proud to say that Hamiltonians were in the vanguard of Canadians who contributed time, effort and money in alleviating the plight of Vietnamese refugees. As one of an earlier group of boat people I know how grateful we all are to Canada for granting the opportunity to build a new life in this great nation.
Having said this, I should like to add a few words of comment. One gets the impression at times that anything but blind acceptance of present immigration policies as they relate to refugees is to be viewed as being in poor taste. But if there are valid questions to be asked-and there are-not all of them are being asked by racist, red-necked crackpots who lack compassion for those less fortunate. There are some questions to be asked pertaining to racial balance or imbalance and I do

The Address-Mr. Beattie
not think they are all being asked by racist, red-necked crackpots. There are two sides to this important question and 1 believe each should be listened to.
On a more serious note, the possibility exists that there will no longer be a Canada to open its doors to anyone if we do not resolve our internal disputes. What does the future hold for Canada and Canadians? I listened to the former prime minister talking yesterday about famous Liberals and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) talking about Sir John A. Macdonald. I should like to go back to Georges Etienne Cartier, one of the founding fathers of confederation and a favourite of mine who, when asked what he thought was going to happen, said "We are going to build a new nation and a new nationality". Sir, Cartier meant that this country would be Canada and that the nationality would be Canadian. We cannot settle for anything less than that.
We must divorce ourselves from those who conveniently forget that Canada was created despite the great problems of geography. It has been held together for more than 100 years by the free will, determination, courage, tolerance, understanding and sacrifice of the vast majority of citizens in every province. Anyone who would seek to gain political ends by provoking one part of the country against another must accept a very grave responsibility. Surely, it is the duty of every member in this House to promote Canada as a country unrivalled in its opportunities for freedom, security, wealth and equality. I am convinced that the will and the attitude of the people of all the provinces will determine whether these two great benefits, opportunity and equality, are to be destroyed, whether our nation is to break up in separate packages. For my own part, I subscribe to the theory presented on provincial equality and national unity by A. R. Kirby, who proclaims that Quebec knows, just as all of Canada knows save for a wilfully self-blinded but influential few, that the constant placation of la belle province for these many, many years is not because of our respect for its culture, the so-called "French fact" and so on. The core of the truth is that we are scared stiff of the alternative to what we recoginize as our present Canadian unity.
I believe Quebec knows its identity and its destiny, or thinks it does, which amounts to the same thing. Some other provinces may also have reached the same point. What this country needs now is not the grovelling, snivelling, sentimental plea of appeasement which only insults the dignity of Quebeckers and tramples whatever shreds of our own dignity that remain. Instead, we need the quiet self-assurance and courage which enable us to say: "This is who we are, and this is where we are going. If you think your interests will be best served by staying with us and sharing the journey, you are welcome to be aboard. We will be happy to have you. We would be lost without you. As you see, we respect you and your wish to preserve your heritage and your cultural identity. However, if you decide to come with us, we expect reciprocal respect from you for the many languages and cultures which exist in the other provinces."

Mr. Speaker, culture should not have to be propped up to controlled. Culture, like religion, is a private matter and will survive according to the devotion of its own adherents, not by false and abrasive artifices. Thus, in genuine mutual respect we can go forward in search of a future we have voluntarily sought as partners, rather than as cohabitants unwillingly bonded only by our fears.
I was delighted to hear the word "individual" permeate the throne speech and to hear the word "opportunity" in the speeches of some hon. members following that. I say this because I believe "individual" and "opportunity" are the two key words in the Canadian system, a sort of Canadian ideal, if you like. In my opinion, the most beaten up word in the Canadian system is "equality", mentioned by the previous speaker. All over this country I have seen people trying to translate the word and make it mean something else. By the wildest stretch of the imagination the people who founded this country, the founders of confederation, never expected everyone to go up the ladder of success the same distance. But they must have the opportunity to go as far as the next individual, and as individuals they have the right to put their foot on the first rung of that ladder and to go as high and as far as their ability, their willingness to work and some breaks will take them. When you have that in Canada, you have guaranteed opportunity; and when you have opportunity in Canada, then you have equality.
I think that is the least we can do for our people, and I think it is important that we at least recognize that fact rather than adopt the gloomy outlook of some of the members of the opposition that this government will destroy the Canadian system in, my goodness, four months! The danger, as I see it, is that we will be unable to transmit the system to future generations, not just this government but all of us. To put it another way, the system will not fail us but some of us might fail the system.
Today our country is facing big problems, but then which country is not? Most Canadians are bewildered by these problems, used as we are to constant growth, regular productivity increases, an unlimited supply of natural resources and social benefits. But occasionally one gets the impression that those who maintain that the world owes them a living are going to win. On top of all this, everyone seems to be blaming everyone else for this turn in our fortunes. While I agree that we may be faced with difficult times ahead, I cannot see anything being gained by encouraging the growth of a feeling of defeatism. The problems that must be dealt with call for a sense of confidence, a sense of hope and a spirit of courage and determination to succeed. We must refuse to let the odd setback interfere with our long range goal of a united and prosperous Canada.
The method of achieving this goal brings me to the story of a great Canadian. I am indebted to Kenneth Bagnell for this story. In one of Pierre Berton's recent and vivid books "My Country" there is a story of Samuel Hearne, from the same
October 11, 1979

province as the former speaker, a man whose life was filled with risk, who stands in contrast to the mood of many people of our own generation who seem given more and more to caution, hesitation and second thoughts. Hearne was a magnificent risk taker. In 1769 when he was 24 years old, he set out on foot on a trek of 4,000 miles across the hard and lonely land from northern Manitoba to the shores of the western Arctic in search of a fabled copper mine. Hearne was almost completely inexperienced. Along the way he was robbed once, he had to turn back twice, and toward the end of the expedition he witnessed a massacre of helpless Eskimos. In the end there was no copper mine. His journey took seven years 24 months and seven days. He managed to produce, despite the ordeal, a journal en route that is a classic to this day. Hearne's real contribution, writes Berton-
-was his close and accurate description of the Chipewyan and Dogrib Indians, the flora and fauna of the country through which he travelled and his willingness to adapt to native ways, which set the pattern of Arctic survival for generations.
It is obvious that the days of that special kind of risk, one man pitted against the elements, have passed into history. But in recent years, among many of our people there seems to be a growing awareness of risk of any kind. With few exceptions, our generation is making a high virtue out of caution. Some who recognize this claim that it has grown out of despair, specifically American despair brought on by the assassination of leaders, the ordeal of Vietnam and the disgrace of Watergate. That gloom, I suggest, has touched all of us, for if the morale of such a close neighbour is lowered, it is natural that our own will be affected.
The causes for the timidity around us, however, lie beyond the recent American past; they are historic and worldwide. They may be the result of a century that has been disappointing, of wars that were futile, alliances that were doomed and dreams of world brotherhood that did not materialize. Beyond these, there has been a disappointment in science which has not cured all our ills, in education which has not solved all our problems, in political promises made but not fulfilled. This series of frustrations, one after the other, has created a climate in which it is easy to retreat, to lose the willingness to venture.
It is not hard to find reasons for prudence, to set aside the old maxim "nothing ventured, nothing gained" and to replace it with another which sounds just as wise, "nothing ventured, nothing lost". This passive and defensive mood is reflected, in some ways at least, in the growing trust we give to the opinions of people we call futurists, recent professionals, often commanding large fees, who tell us what lies ahead, so that the risk of experiment and adventure are diminished.
Now, in the field of economics in which issues are growing more and more complex this care may be necessary and wise, but when it becomes the philosophy by which people live so that courage is replaced by caution and energy by inertia, then life is lessened and generations to come are defrauded. Some of the hesitation about making a bold decision or setting upon a new course arises out of a fear that we may make the wrong decision or take the undesired course. While this may be a natural inclination, it is nonetheless weak. Too many of our
The Address-Mr. Beattie
organizations, business, labour and government, are kept from reaching their high ambitions because within them are men and women who, when called upon to make an adventuresome decision, waver because they are frightened of being wrong. They misunderstand.
Thomas Edison, it is said, once experimented over many months without success. Someone working alongside him sympathized, saying that it was too bad to have to work so hard, so long, without results. "But", Edison said, "we have a lot of results. We now know 700 things that don't work". Samuel Hearne was sent, in one sense, on an expedition that was a mistake. There was no copper to be mined on the rim of the Arctic and the fabled Northwest Passage of which his employers dreamed was of little value. His chief findings, as Pierre Berton notes, were negative but they were nevertheless meaningful.
Nothing could be more wrong than for people to believe that the prevalent mood of retrenchment is acceptable, for the main trouble with an attitude of retreat is that it feeds on itself and becomes self-fulfilling. People who go on the defensive, whether in relation to the future of our country or the future of their own lives, find it more and more difficult to change their attitude and to take new initiative. There are people, of course, who have given up, who believe that the signs of the times are so ominous, populations exploding and habitable land decreasing, that it is naive to expect man to hold on to courage and to act in constructive and creative ways.
This, however, is not what history has shown, for in both nations and individuals the great contributions to history have always been in the midst of circumstances that were, on the surface, far from conducive. We have a choice. A discouraging time can bring paralysis or stimulus. That was clearly the case in the light of one Nathaniel Hawthorne who travelled a difficult road before he found the key to triumph. Hawthorne wrote a sentence significant for all whose dreams are temporarily at bay. He said:
An individual must keep faith in himself while the incredulous world assails him with its utter disbelief.
I have people say to me once in a while, "How do you defend taking strong stands on things and having strong convictions?" I have reached the point now of telling them that I have spent all my adult life trying to reduce my ignorance. I have gained a body of knowledge from people here and from people who have preceded me. I am not ashamed to say that occasionally 1 go to the source of all truths, the scriptures. I have a way of life now which kind of works and I can defend it.
I ask my fellow members how we are going to convince our Canadian brothers about the great equality of opportunity which exists in our country today, opportunities magnified in a united and prosperous Canada, if we do not have the courage of our own convictions. It will take courage, a special kind of courage. However, I have travelled this world and I have studied history and I can simply find no great contributions

October 1 1, 1979
The Address-Mr. Lapierre
made by those of placid faith and cringing courage. Only those with abiding beliefs are the ones who look ahead of the time and make any imprint in history. We must give people something that endures.
My plea today is for us not to rob our generation of the power which comes with simple abiding belief in oneself and in one's country. The capacity for that kind of belief and courage is not something a country or its leaders can set in motion, the way it can set in motion controls upon wages and prices. Our people must be encouraged to rediscover their natural gifts, their human gifts and their true potential, realizing at the same time that there is no heavier burden than a great potential. Also they can be asked to remember that their country has achieved its character in the face of great odds and continues in spite of great difficulties, and they can be reminded from time to time of their abiding strength.
Donald Alexander Smith who drove the last spike on the CPR said:
Canadians have always stood for courage and unconquerability. They have the muscle, the wholesomeness of life, the strength of will.
It should be clear to all of us that we have already entered into Canada's most critical period. The wisest among us cannot predict the outcome, but we know we have the resource to face it and to see it through in constructive ways. What all our people need now is a renewal of our confidence in the human spirit and its reach. In the end that may matter more than anything else. Mr. Wilfred Grenfell said the following:
It is courage the world needs, not infallibility. Courage is always the surest wisdom.
Like enthusiasm it is contagious. It must be kept on display. But we cannot kindle the fire of courage and enthusiasm in the heart of another human being unless it burns brightly within our own. That fire burns in our bellies or we would not be here. It is transferable. We must reach the hearts and the minds of people who would despair in the sordidness and cynicism of our times, individuals who look to us for help, leadership and a display of courage which will keep this great country of Canada united and prosperous.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at the outset to extend to you my sincere congratulations for your nomination. The fact that hon. members designated you a second time to sit in the chair in spite of the present circumstances is a proof of your impartiality, efficiency and wisdom.
I also want to congratulate the two movers of the address and assure the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) that as a part of a new generation of members of the House, 1 am just like him dedicated to keeping the country united and strong.
It is a privilege and a great honour for me to make this first speech in the name of the people of the riding of Shefford who, after having been represented for more than 11 years by a

member of the Social Credit Party of Canada, have come back to their long time Liberal tradition. I hope that this tradition will be kept for many years. Following the footsteps of parliamentarians like Huntington, Parmelee, Boivin, Leclerc and Neveu is for me a very important challenge and I hope I will take it up successfully.
Let me thank most heartfully my constituents of Shefford for the confidence they have put in me, and I want to assure them of my most assiduous devotion and of my determination to defend their interests in the House. According to the tradition, when a new member of parliament makes his maiden speech in this House, he does his best to describe the beauty and the charm of his constituency. I would like to describe the beauty of the eastern townships, but since that beauty cannot be described, I would rather invite my colleagues to come and visit our beautiful region. If we consider the numerous visits that the new Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) made to our region in the last two years, we must conclude that the Progressive Conservatives did like my constituency but, unfortunately for them, my constituency did not like them.
To come to the Speech from the Throne, I must acknowledge that, probably because I am the youngest of all members,
I was still deluding myself about the determination and the sensitivity of this new government faced with the problems which preoccupy Canadians in general and more particularly the voters in my constituency. Unfortunately, after having heard, read and read again that speech, I only feel bitterly disappointed. While the former government was called breathless, I call this one asthmatic. For me, to take over four months to prepare such a poor program of action is a sign of general weakness and asthma. As an example, I would like to recall the expectations of Canadian farmers since the May 22 election and show the inaction of this government.
Just a few days after the election, everybody was waiting impatiently for the appointment of that super minister of agriculture who was, according to what the new Prime Minister had said, to hold a very high rank within the cabinet, precisely in order to improve the status of farmers. What a disappointment it was for us to realize that the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) was not even admitted within the closed circle of the most important cabinet ministers.
With the milk producers, I waited in vain to hear the announcement that there would be a drastic cut in cheese imports. With them, I have come to realize once again that the government does not keep its promises. With the pork producers, especially, I have been waiting for the energetic measures that were promised with a view to encouraging the sale of their products abroad. In that field, as in the others, our hopes were dashed. With the whole agricultural sector, I have been waiting for an increase in the funds allotted to research and development. There again, the government has changed its
October 11, 1979

mind. Mr. Speaker, those many commitments having been betrayed, I felt sure that the government was saving the best for the Speech from the Throne. But alas! The height of deception was reached when His Excellency the Governor General failed to even mention once the word "agriculture". Let me tell you that for a party that was supposed to raise the status of agriculture, this is a very discreet way of doing so.
Worse still, the government says it is prepared to introduce in the House a bill to help settle more quickly labour disputes under federal jurisdiction, whereas current statutes do allow the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) to intervene into disputes that have been lasting for too long. I will give only one example: the dispute in the Montreal harbour. Farmers have been asking the minister to step in for many months now, but he keeps saying no and disregards their appeals. If this is how they raise the status of agriculture, then I deeply question the intentions of this government.
Mr. Speaker, although agriculture is a vital matter for the people in my riding, I would be remiss if I did not refer to other aspects of the Speech from the Throne which attracted my attention.
My age allows me to share the worry and concern of young Canadians faced by their job prospects, their future. That is why 1 welcome with pleasure, but also with a little reserve, the government's intention to create a youth employment secretariat. But I am afraid this could only be a new name for some old agencies. I hope the axe of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) will not prevent this new agency from playing a really efficient part in the fight against unemployment.
By refusing to earmark funds for the Canada Works program in my riding, this government has put a number of young and not so young people out of work. 1 hope that programs will be created as soon as possible to enable the idle but powerful hands in our society to join the labour market and thus contribute to building our country.
I am much concerned by the review of the Unemployment Insurance Act and I hope the government no longer intends to apply its discriminatory concept of variable benefits. I have already communicated my views to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) and I hope he will take them into consideration.
Industrial development is also an important issue in my region and I urge the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacKay) not to wait for his mandate to be extended by Parliament before reviewing the delimitation of areas designated for grants. The riding of Shefford must recover its status of designated area to respond fully to the challenge launched by the Prime Minister yesterday to build our country. I consider that change so important that I asked to meet the minister responsible to explain to him in detail the validity of our representations. I hope that my request will be favourably considered.
The Address-Mr. Faour
Another significant aspect for development and employment in our area is the proposed decentralization of the cartography services of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in the vicinity of Sherbrooke. That big project announced by the previous government has been shifted over to the "deferred" files in the office of the President of the Treasury Board. I speak now on behalf of my colleagues from the eastern townships to ask what this government intends to do now. I would say that I am relying now on the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle) who holds the important office of Minister of Supply and Services, in the hands of the Progressive Conservative Party now, to inform us on the future of this project.
I also take this opportunity to comment on the now famous and unique speech of the no less unique minister of state for social programs, his address to the Federation des clubs de Page d'or du Quebec. Here is what he said to those people: "Our country can no longer afford to wander in the field of universal benefits and must concentrate its efforts on those who are the most in need without, however, jeopardizing its economy and the situation of those who depend on the present system."
These few words have caused much concern and insecurity among our senior citizens, because to question universal entitlement to old age security would be, in the eyes of many Canadians, a retrograde and anti-social move. I hope that the disappearance of the honorific title of this minister will result in the disappearance of this theory which would take away from Canadians the prospect of a secure future at the time of their retirement.
In closing, I join with my right hon. leader in asking the government to create a truly national spirit and to introduce programs which do not mean a shirking of all its responsibilities. Nothing in the Speech from the Throne shows the coherent vision of tomorrow's Canada that my colleagues and myself in the official opposition can offer to our fellow citizens of Quebec for the referendum. We do not believe that the Utopian feelings of this government, which can lead it to believe that there can be any spirit of co-operation between a central government and a government of secession, could promote the cause of federalism in Quebec. This attitude of neglect towards separatism will certainly be compensated by the energy and the vigour with which we, on this side of the House, intend to fight this battle.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the government party, in view of its extreme fragility, will be willing to accept a few of the suggestions made by the opposition and show some realism in the best interests of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fonse Faour (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel quite honoured today to make my first speech of this session. It is not my maiden speech and I guess you could say that I am a member of that small "class of '78",

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Faour
having arrived here about this time last year. It is a fairly short time since I made my own maiden speech. I should like to congratulate the mover of the motion before us and the seconder, as well as those other new members who have spoken on this motion in respect of the throne speech.
It is always a very significant occasion when an hon. member makes his maiden speech, at least it was when I made mine in this House. I trust that for all of those new members this will be the beginning of an interesting and rewarding career. I was going to add the word "long", but perhaps I should reserve that for members of my own party.
I should also like to congratulate those hon. members who have returned here. It is interesting to note how the composition of the House has changed. It is interesting to see different faces opposite at this time.
My comments today will present a perspective from my point of view of Atlantic Canada, with emphasis on my own riding and my own province of Newfoundland.
Before commencing those comments I should like to present my own impression of what I have witnessed in the House in the last few days, those few days the House has been in session since the election. I find it astounding that two parties have basically changed positions in the House and seem to have reversed themselves in terms of policy as well. It is incredible that the former opposition party, now the party in government, is promulgating policies and programs it criticized not more than five months ago. It is equally incredible that the party on this side of the House to my right, which was the government only five months ago, is criticizing the present government for proposing the same policies it was implementing five months ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is perhaps a fact that I am a little naive, Mr. Speaker, being still a relatively new member, just having a little less than a year in the House under my belt. Perhaps it is naive to think that political parties are supposed to stick to their convictions. If that is naivete, Mr. Speaker, I hope it remains with me for quite a while.
My comments today about Atlantic Canada have been prefaced by the comments of the former leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), when he stated during the election campaign that regional development would be at the very centre of national policy, whereas under the Liberals it had been given secondary importance. That is a very significant commitment by the Prime Minister to the people of Atlantic Canada. For many years we in Altantic Canada have had a problem in making our presence felt on the national scene, and certainly in making our presence felt among those in the government of the day, in spite of the fact that as members of the government, whether Liberal or Tory, there have been and are many from Atlantic Canada. Over the past years the Atlantic region has just not had a voice or input into the program and policies of government, a voice and input needed by the Atlantic region in order to make it a contributing part of this country we call Canada.

In that regard I was encouraged by what the Prime Minister said before the election, that regional development, in particular Atlantic development, would be a priority of this government. The government has only been in power for four and a half months but they have already reneged on that promise. Their record has been dismal in that time in terms of placing priority on regional development and Atlantic development in their programs. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is supposed to be an instrument of government policy for furthering the development of the underdeveloped regions, in particular the Atlantic region. But how can the Prime Minister say that it is a priority of his government if the minister responsible for DREE is not even within the inner cabinet?
The throne speech places regional development in the forefront as a concern of the government. I do not claim that in that speech the government was listing its priorities, but it would be nice if regional development were listed as one of the five priorities of the government. But their record of the past four odd months has shown otherwise and in fact regional development is not a priority of this government. The Atlantic region can expect no more from this government than they received from the previous government.
The government has not pursued a policy of full employment. Although the Atlantic region has the highest rate of unemployment in the country, there has been no real attack on this particular problem. All that the government has proposed, and it is all that we have heard about in the media over the last four months, are cutbacks, spending restraint, privatization and so on. The government seems to feel that by spending less the unemployed in Atlantic Canada will somehow go away, that maybe they will go to some other country or another part of Canada. However, the problem will not go away just by the government wishing it away.
Positive action must be taken, but in the past four and a half months not one new job has been created by this government. There has not even been a review, a study or a royal commission formed to study the particular problems of the Atlantic region. The only review affecting the Atlantic region in particular was done by the Department of Employment and Immigration, and it was not of a positive nature. There was no review of programs to create jobs or economic development. What we had was a review of to what extent the government should further attack the unemployed in the region.
Specifically that review, that restrictive document issued by the department, called into question and asked for a review of the entitlement of seasonal workers, fishermen and others, to unemployment benefits. There was no discussion at all of jobs to alleviate the unemployment problem in a positive way. There was no discussion of what these people will do if they are disentitled to unemployment benefits, people such as workers in the fish plants and in the tourist industry. The guiding light of this government has been a slavish adherence to the dogma of "spend less". Any first-year economic student would
October 11, 1979

tell them that that policy is foolish, but I will pursue that area a little later.
The government expressed its commitment to regional development in April during the election campaign, but how has this been expressed over the last few months? One needs only to look at the negative effects of their spending restraint policies since that time. As I mentioned before, the biggest problem in economic terms in Atlantic Canada is unemployment.
I have here the statistics on the unemployment rates of a few months ago. The official unemployment rate for Newfoundland was 18.8 per cent, 14.3 per cent for Prince Edward Island and 13.4 per cent for New Brunswick. If those figures are contrasted with the western provinces, for example, Alberta was at 4.9 per cent, Saskatchewan at 5.8 per cent and Ontario at an unemployment rate of 7.4 per cent. Statistics Canada confirmed what we had known all along last year when they came out with the concept of hidden unemployment. If one looks at the hidden unemployment figures for the Atlantic region, the rate jumps to 32.9 per cent in Newfoundland and 27.3 per cent in Prince Edward Island.
Those particular figures only tell part of the story. Let us look at the job availability statistics in the region. Whereas Alberta had over 64 jobs for every 100 residents age 15 and over, the maritimes average only 44 jobs. In terms of the unemployed there were nine jobs for every 100 people unemployed last year. Nothing has been done to solve the problem at all. Instead the government has embarked on another systematic attack on the unemployed.
I say "another" because the Liberal government initiated the first attack last fall. The Liberal government introduced Bill C-14 last fall, which amounted to a vicious kick to the unemployed. Present government members opposed that bill quite strongly, but where are they now? The present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) is across the way, and he said during the debate on the bill that it amounted to a kick in the gut to the unemployed. We agreed with him. At that time we were arguing the same side of the issue and we felt that priority should be given to fighting unemployment, not the unemployed. We felt that unemployment was the enemy, not those of our constituents who happened to be without jobs. They were not the enemy.

speechtext:
It does not make any sense to me to say that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) and Bay Street are deciding policies for Atlantic Canada, where the results are absolutely tragic. After May 22 when the Tories became the government, they forgot about their concern for the unemployed in Atlantic Canada and proclaimed this very regulation that they had fought. And as if that were not bad enough, they then reviewed the entitlement of seasonal workers, fishermen and so on. No job-creation programs have been presented nor have any proposals for economic development been presented, but there have been plans to cut back on benefits for the unemployed and other underprivileged people in the country.
The Speech from the Throne referred to other cutbacks under the guise of streamlining spending. It is amazing how sweet words like "streamlining spending" can camouflage for weak minds the havoc that is wreaked on individuals by an insensitive government. Mr. Speaker, this government is dedicated to a mindless pursuit of a mindless ideology. It is obvious that it is no more a friend of the unemployed than was its predecessor. This new review will make it an even greater enemy of the unemployed.

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Faour
Some hon. members opposite are from the Atlantic region and I know they appreciate the problem. Frankly, I do not understand how they can rationalize their membership in that party. Hon. members opposite from other regions of the country would do well to visit communities in Atlantic Canada to see the beauty down there, to enjoy the friendliness and hospitality of the people. At the same time they could see what this type of policy means to individual Canadians there and to the children of workers caught in this bind.
In the debate on this issue last year I said that it would mean cold homes and hungry children. Mr. Speaker, I have just completed a tour of my riding and 1 can see that there are going to be cold homes and hungry children this winter because of the regulations promulgated by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. If the government pursues this policy, 8,700 Newfoundland fishermen on the south coast of the island, on the west coast of the island and on the northeast coast of the island-not counting the number affected in the other three maritime provinces-will be placed on provincial welfare rolls.
I will return to the original thread of my comments today, Mr. Speaker, which is to ask if this is what the government regards as placing a high priority on regional Atlantic development. If it is, I am certainly glad they have not placed a low priority on it.
The government's attitude of restraint at any cost does not make sense when applied to the economic situation in Atlantic Canada. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) was a member of the opposition and the House was debating Bill C-19 in November, 1976, he said:
It is beyond my comprehension how any government can restrain expenditures in an area of the country which has an unemployment rate of 13.9 per cent.
It was lower then than now, Mr. Speaker. He continued:
It is, in fact, positively cruel and inhuman for any government to apply a restraint policy equally across this country as though every section of it is the same. It may be a policy of restraint that is quite apt for provinces like Ontario, Alberta or Saskatchewan, perhaps, where there are now high employment figures, but it is not proper to apply it blindly to Newfoundland which has an unemployment rate of almost 14 per cent.
At that time the unemployment rate was only 14 per cent in Newfoundland but today it is 18 per cent. This leads us to ask why a restraint policy must now apply holus-bolus across the board to Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians as well as to Albertans and people in Saskatchewan. This appears to me to be contrary to the expressed promise of the Prime Minister for Atlantic regional development. He seemed to place a high priority on such development. This would seem to me to mean special policies tailored to individual areas of the country, particularly the Atlantic region.
As an aside, Mr. Speaker, I would remark that hon. members opposite at least seem to be demonstrating some interest in the plight of Atlantic Canada by their presence in the House today. When I look to my right to the Liberal benches, however, I see only three members. If this is a demonstration of their interest in the Atlantic provinces, it is no wonder that the party to which I belong is on the increase in Newfoundland

and Nova Scotia. It is also probably the reason for the lack of action during the last 16 years under a Liberal government. The Tories cannot take any consolation from that, however, because for the past four and one-half months they have not stayed with the ideas and policies they presented while in opposition.
As I pointed out, when the Minister of Finance was in opposition he stated it was madness to apply this type of policy right across the country without making exceptions for areas such as the Atlantic region. Yet that is what is happening right now. The Atlantic region is caught in the bind imposed by this cutback mentality, this restraint program that is affecting the lives of Canadians all over the country. In Atlantic Canada it will mean more unemployment and hardship, especially this winter.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister stated that regional development would be a priority of this government, but its over-all policy has turned out to be to the detriment of Atlantic Canada. When we examine some of the government's programs on the national level it is easy to see how disastrous they will be for Atlantic Canada.
The leader of this party questioned the Minister of Finance this morning on the matter of interest rate hikes. This will further depress the already depressed economy of the Atlantic region. If this policy creates problems in the stock market in Toronto it is easy to imagine what a problem it will be for consumers, small businessmen and fishermen in Atlantic Canada. It strikes at the heart of economic activity ail over the country. The government has not seen fit to introduce programs designed to alleviate the effects of interest rate hikes. The problem presented to Atlantic Canada in this respect is even greater than that presented to the rest of the country, yet the government has not produced any offsetting programs for that area.
The whole thrust of the government's policies has been to exclude the Atlantic region. The biggest plank in the Tory platform in the last year or so was first mortgage interest deductibility, and later a mortgage tax credit, but that totally bypasses Atlantic Canada where over 70 per cent of the people are ineligible. In the final year of the program the government will spend over $2 billion, yet it not only has minimal effects in the Atlantic region but has already been cancelled out by the interest hike. How does a government that stated regional development as a high priority justify this type of expenditure?
I will be interested to hear what the government present on this subject in the next few months.
Another area of cutback that will have serious impact in my part of the country concerns the moneys that were allocated to the development of small craft harbours for fishermen through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Hundreds of fishermen in my riding and that of the hon. members from Cape Breton will be affected. I would be interested to know why no allowance was made for this industry which is so crucial to the Atlantic region when the government has a stated policy of regional development as a priority. It is imperative, particularly in Newfoundland where harbour development has been
October 11, 1979

behind the other Atlantic provinces, that the priority attached by the Prime Minister to regional development be demonstrated in this area. We are not getting that. We are getting the "happy hacker from Bay Street". His influence and effect is being felt in every fishing harbour in Newfoundland and in the maritime provinces.
In this particular area many projects are needed and many more need to be completed. There are thousands of fishermen depending on this particular program for their livelihood. In these areas the Tories opposite are showing themselves to be carbon copies of the Liberals on this side. They are continuing to implement Liberal-Tory policies and promises that have detrimental effects on the Atlantic region, and they are continuing to pay only lip service to regional development in the eastern provinces. That is obviously all that the former leader of the opposition, now Prime Minister, meant when he talked in the spring about placing regional development as a priority.
What areas can we suggest that the government work on? The Liberals' refusal to make a commitment to the steel industry in Cape Breton was one area, and the Tories seem quite reluctant as well. If the government would provide the economic leadership, this area has the potential totally to transform certainly the Cape Breton economy as well as the economy of Nova Scotia. We have seen no new initiatives in terms of ending discriminatory transportation policies in the region. There has been no departure, certainly on the part of the government, from the user-pay policy which was the philosophy of the former government.

I hope the same thing is going to happen to this government fairly quickly too.
Transportation policy is the major tool that the government has at its disposal to stimulate development. We have seen nothing in terms of a study in the area, let alone some activity.
The other major tool is energy policy. The Atlantic region has the highest energy costs in the country. Not only does it present hardship for consumers, but also it has to have a stultifying and stunting effect on the growth and development in the areas as well. In terms of saying that regional development is a priority for this government, energy policy has to be right up there with transportation and fisheries policy for the Atlantic region. Energy policy is probably more important because it takes energy to run trucks, trains and fishing boats. So 1 say that energy policy is crucial yet this government has done nothing in terms of solving the Atlantic region's energy problems.
We have heard talk of energy self-sufficiency in 1990 and deals with Mr. Lougheed, but have heard nothing in terms of policies to balance the real problem which Atlantic Canada faces. To his credit, and 1 say this quite openly, the Prime Minister has agreed to provincial jurisdiction over offshore resources, unlike the former government. This is very impor-
The Address-Mr. Faour
tant to the future energy requirements on the east coast. That is not the only answer. The granting of provincial jurisdiction has to be seen as part of an over-all energy policy for the region. There is no evidence at all that the government has even broached the question of a maritime energy policy. Not only that, but in terms of their disastrous policy concerning Petro-Canada, the long-term energy security of the eastern provinces is seriously threatened and undermined.
I am not going to go into detail about Petro-Canada. My leader has already done that in his reply to the Speech from the Throne. I would like to speak briefly about the particular concerns of the region with regard to the effect PetroCan has on it. Petro-Canada has been involved in the search for oil deposits off the east coast. It has been involved in the Sable Island discovery and in the Hibernia well off St. John's that was said to be so promising a few weeks ago. It has been involved in 80 per cent of the wells that have been drilled off the coast of Labrador. For eastern Canada our dependence on imported oil makes it imperative that Petro-Canada protect our interests. We need that corporation to do that.
We propose as well-and this has important significance to Newfoundland-that the oil refinery that is now in Newfoundland lying dormant at Come-By-Chance should be taken over by Petro-Canada. It makes common sense. There are benefits for Newfoundland and for eastern Canada. First, it will provide security of energy supply for eastern Canada. Secondly, that security of supply would provide security of employment for people in Newfoundland.
I am just about to end my speech, Mr. Speaker, and I know that my time has just about run out, but I do want to emphasize that Petro-Canada should be expanded in this area as a fundamental part of the energy policy in the Atlantic region.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to participate in this debate. It is a privilege I have enjoyed since I was first elected to Parliament in June, 1957.
1 wish to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address. They gave a worthy account of themselves, and in my view they are a credit to the constituencies which elected them to this House.
I wish also to congratulate Mr. Speaker on his reappointment, which is an honour I believe he has earned and richly deserves.
I also wish to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the members of the cabinet on the quality of the proposals put forward in the throne speech, the first of a set of new proposals put forward by a Conservative government in, I think, 16 years. I believe the measures which have been earmarked for consideration reflect the careful thought and planning which took place between the dissolution of Parliament and the election of the new government. 1 believe that the legislation, when implemented, will be beneficial to all Canadians.
Unlike some hon. members who have already participated in this debate, I am pleased that the new government took a little extra time to prepare its legislative package. I say this because I have a long memory, and I well remember Canadians-and even today-suffering from the hasty actions of a previous administration, which hoped to be all things to all people in its planned "sixty days of decision".
Down Lunenburg way our oldest citizens have a saying which I suppose our forebears brought with them when they came over from Europe in 1753. It goes something like this: "The hurrier I go the behinder I get". So I hope that the careful, thought-out approach to our problems evidenced by the government will be the hallmark of this new administration.
While this year marks 112 years of parliamentary government in Canada, a record of which we can all be proud, it is worth nothing that a good friend and neighbour of Canada's is this year celebrating 250 years of parliamentary rule. I refer to the Commonwealth of the Bahamas, which celebrated this event with the opening of Parliament in Nassau on Saturday, September 29. The years from 1729 to 1979 have seen a tremendous evolution in the Bahamas not only in Parliament but also socially and economically. They have moved from a farming and fishing community to a tourist based economy with banking and finance becoming an important part of the economic life of the country. They also moved from representative government to responsible government and then to

full independence from Britain. In 1967, although it cannot be said, strictly speaking, that it was a parliamentary change, the country experienced what we perhaps would call a quiet revolution when the white minority government was overthrown by a black majority government which was then instituted. This change, more than any other, showed the importance of the vote and the significance of ensuring that each adult person in the country be granted this important right.
1 was privileged to represent Canada at the two hundred and fiftieth anniversary celebrations, and the interest taken in this event not only by members of the Commonwealth but by other countries as well was outstanding. From the minute you arrive in Nassau you cannot help but be aware of the fact that racial tensions there today between blacks and whites are non-existent.
I view this as a tremendous accomplishment which we and other countries would do well to strive to emulate.
When we look at what is happening today in Cuba, for example, and review the statements made by the so-called non-aligned countries at the recent conference held in Havana,
I hope hon. members will agree with me when I say that the Commonwealth of the Bahamas stands out like a bright and shining jewel in what is becoming a very troubled sea, the Caribbean, and the importance of this area will grow considerably in our immediate future.
As the struggle for power intensifies in the Caribbean, where it is now evident Communist forces are on the increase, especially in Cuba, it is a welcome relief to note the importance attached by the Bahamians to parliamentary democracy. This condition exists, 1 believe, because of the respect that is shown by the people to their elected representatives and to the church. They believe that of all God's creations, people are the most important. We are made in His image, and we have been given definite rights and freedoms. As part of God's plan we do not exist alone. We are placed in communities, and our orderly and just development and our prosperity and happiness must be the concern of each other. They believe that it is for this very purpose that Parliaments exist, to provide opportunities for orderly developments. It is for this reason that they respect parliamentary democracy and pledge themselves to its continuation in the future, upholding it in the face of all onslaughts.
I believe that a democratic Parliament has the right to expect the trust, respect and support of all its citizens. Parliamentary democracy cannot function satisfactorily unless it receives this support. By the same token, an awesome responsibility is laid upon members of Parliament. It is a position of great honour and dignity, and I submit that it must not be taken lightly. It necessitates a respect for traditions and for the ideals of the institution as well as a willingness to work and advance its future. It also necessitates a willingness to maintain a relationship with constituents and to take seriously their well-being.
Just as reasonable support of Parliament must be an integral part of its functioning and well-being, so must constructive criticism from the political opposition as well as from support-
October 11, 1979

ers of the party in power be accepted and expected as a vital ingredient of the democratic process. All human beings require constructive, objective evaluation in order to perform efficiently and effectively, and this is no less true of members of Parliament.
In many areas of the world today the democratic parliamentary process is under severe attack, or it is even being supplanted. This, unfortunately, is happening because Parliaments have failed to live up to their ideals. They have not provided opportunities for all the people they represent. A dissatisfied people will quickly seek that system that will fulfil its needs. Here in Canada I believe we must be especially concerned that all of our people have an opportunity for full human development, most especially in the fields of education and economics. Our system must make certain that opportunities for employment and medical care are available to everyone as far as it is economically feasible. Parliament, through its legislation and its influence, must do all in its power to promote the peace, unity and happiness of the Canadian people.
Divisions caused by language, race, colour, creed, geographical location or social standing, 1 submit, must never be supported. Within the democratic system there will be differences of political persuation. We see them right here in this House. But these must not be allowed to divide us permanently or to prevent justice from being carried out. From the very beginning Parliament has based its existence upon Christian principles as well as the principles of democracy and the rule of law. When these principles are abandoned the authority and the respect of Parliament will be undermined, and the rights and freedoms of individuals will be abused. The parliamentary government of this country has brought us this far, and it is my hope that the members of this Parliament who are deeply concerned and conscious of the fundamental rights and freedoms of all our citizens will work assiduously toward making Canada a just, united and prosperous country.
The throne speech, in my opinion, goes a long way toward accomplishing this dream, toward making it a reality. The proposals put forward truly represent a change of direction for Canada as we enter the 1980s. It is good for all of us to hear that consultation and co-operation will be the hallmarks of the new era. This will be a pleasant change, I submit, from what we have known in the past. We saw evidence of the type of consultation and co-operation which will exist when this Parliament opened on Tuesday. The time has come to reconcile our differences and to work together to realize fully our country's potential. By building for the future we can renew the dream of Canadian federalism. We can renew our faith in Canada. We can restore our pride in this country. We can be glad to stand up and say "I am proud to be a Canadian".
