speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In the throne speech this government is demonstrating that it is a government of compassion, for it proposes to extend spouse's allowances in circumstances where they are now denied. It will amend legislation respecting veterans, whose wants for all too long have been overlooked, despite the
The Address-Mr. Crouse
fact that they have made untold sacrifices on behalf of this country. It plans to establish select committees with the resources and powers necessary to inquire fully into the special needs of our handicapped and disabled citizens. One needs only to visit these people in their homes or in the senior citizens' establishments which have been set up across the country to realize that their needs are genuine and worthy of every consideration.
There could be no question that the greatest immediate challenge facing Canada today is to restore growth, confidence and jobs within the Canadian economy. This can only be done by the government and the people working together as a team. The government has pledged to reduce the load on the backs of Canadians through an expenditure management system within government which sets over-all spending limits on all ministers. 1 am pleased to see that in the throne speech because it was a proposal put forward by the present Auditor General, Mr. James Macdonell, during a period when 1 served for two years as chairman of the public accounts committee. It is a measure which is long overdue and should bring about great savings for the Canadian people.
This government plans to offer for private purchase and ownership those Crown corporations operating in areas where direct government intervention is no longer necessary. I think this is a good move for, as Conservatives, we believe that government should not be doing for the people those things people can best do for themselves.
Most important of all, we are going to establish sunset legislation, which will provide Parliament with a regular opportunity to judge whether government programs and agencies should be continued or phased out. As a Nova Scotian I have great respect for that type of legislation because it was in 1918 that Halifax experienced a great explosion, and it was only a few years ago that the mechanism set up to administer funds provided for those injured in that explosion was disbanded. This is what we mean by sunset legislation: examine these Crown corporations and agencies to determine whether they have a job to do, and if they have let them continue doing it; but, if not, disband them and save some of the taxpayers' money.
These moves are only a beginning. We believe individual initiative must be encouraged so as to generate growth and job opportunities. In furtherance of this aim, research and development will be expanded in Canada to promote the export of Canadian goods and services. To help the individual Canadian build a stake in this country we plan to establish a program of tax credits for mortgage interest and property taxes. This one measure alone will go a long way toward stimulating our housing industry while providing new job opportunities for young Canadians.
Unlike the previous speaker, I have read the Speech from the Throne through thoroughly, not once but a number of times, and I believe it gives special recognition to the needs of Atlantic Canada. I say this because it proposes to bring in a

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Crouse
white paper on the future of our fisheries resources prepared in consultation with our fishermen, a large number of whom the previous speaker represents and many of whom 1 represent. There is to be consultation with the fishermen, the fishing industry and the provinces.
As most members are aware, the fishing industry is of fundamental importance to Atlantic Canada and to the wellbeing of a large segment of our people. In my view, there are very few primary industries which at the present time offer opportunities comparable to the fishing industry. Given the right opportunities by way of licences, quotas and markets, for example, our fishermen are capable of doubling their present landed values in a few years. I hope the government when preparing its white paper on the future development of our fisheries resources will give careful consideration to all the problems which presently surround this important industry.
For example, there is a need for extended lines of credit at reasonable interest rates, something the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) will have to examine, to cover the present inflated interest rates brought on by the exorbitant spending of the outfit which was in power before we took over, as a result of which the cost of ship construction and replacement has risen to exorbitant heights. Provision of investment allowances or tax write-offs go a long way toward stimulating ship construction, and while this will be helpful to all classes of operators, the needs of our inshore fishermen as they apply to the construction of public marine works must not be overlooked. In order to ensure that value is received for money expended there must be close liaison with the fishermen and other users, as well as with provincial and local authorities, to ensure the most practical use of wharves, breakwaters, slipways and docking and handling structures. In some areas there are already adequate wharves but unfortunately, due to the action of the sea, they have become silted in and are usable only at high tide. So we have to consider whether further dredging is needed in order to make existing services usable.
I would also point out that it is not sufficient to consider expanding the fishing industry without providing adequate surveillance capacity over our marine resource areas, together with an adequate research and rescue capability to ensure the safety of our fishermen. I hope the white paper will deal also with the need for a better utilization of our shore and sea-based freezer industry and will consider its expansion. If more fish were frozen, processing plants could operate year-round, thereby providing additional employment. I submit we should also examine the need for developing freezer trawlers to preserve catches of presently underutilized species such as silver hake, argentines, offshore herring, mackerel and squid. With oil increasing in price almost monthly it makes no sense whatsoever for our fishermen to throw away these soft species, to throw them back into the sea, especially when they are incidental to a groundfishing operation.
In my constituency one enterprising fishermen has applied for a licence to build a 64-foot freezer trawler so that all the species of catches can be kept in A-l condition prior to landing. When we talk of freezer trawlers we sometimes think

only of huge ships 300 feet or more in length, ice-reinforced and operated on the Hamilton bank off the coast of Labrador. But there are other possibilities for freezer trawlers. It is possible to build a 64-foot freezer trawler and use half the hold for wetfish and have the other half equipped with a freezing unit so that any species caught as incidental to a cod-fishing operation can be put into the freezer section instead of being thrown back into the sea. Everything the fisherman has caught will be utilized and this, I submit, will be vitally necessary as the cost of fishing, especially the cost of oil, continues to escalate.
I submit that the building of these ships will go a long way toward rejuvenating our shipyards and the ancillary business connected with them, while at the same time providing new opportunities for many of our people. This type of program, coupled with the proposals to develop an effective Canadian merchant fleet, should spell the dawn of a new era for all shipbuilding in Canada, and of course this will be vitally important to Atlantic Canada.
It is gratifying to note that the government is committed to making Canada self-sufficient in energy by 1990. That is a start, of course. This government, under the leadership of our new Prime Minister, has already given to Atlantic Canada the right to royalties from any offshore oil and gas developments. We do not know at this stage what this means to our future, but I submit it bodes well for that future.
Due to Canada's national oil policy as announced in February of 1961, Atlantic Canada's energy supply was dominated by imported oil to an extent unequalled in any other region of Canada. In fact, in terms of net energy supply, imported oil accounted in 1976 for an 82 per cent share of our needs compared to 54 per cent in Canada as a whole.
While the problems facing the Atlantic region are apparent, there has been little regional agreement on appropriate solutions. One of the early projects of the Council of Maritime Premiers was the creation of a Maritime Energy Corporation which was supposed to adminster most aspects of energy development in the region. Established on February 16, 1979, after signing a comprehensive agreement covering, among other things, the development of Fundy tidal power, the purchasing of the Point Lepreau nuclear unit and a preferred federal credit rating on all MEC contracts, the whole agreement would now appear to have been scrapped by all parties. I hope, now that the federal government is in new hands and in light of the throne speech promise to stimulate and distribute energy in all its various forms, that we will soon see a reassessment-I direct this request to the new Minister of Finance-a new reassessment of the federal government's role as it applies to the Maritime Energy Corporation. I believe that the strengthening of MEC is important to the development and distribution of electrical energy in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
We need it in order to stimulate tidal power beyond the pilot project presently proposed by the Nova Scotia Tidal Power
October 11, 1979

Corporation at Annapolis. The main purpose of the Annapolis project is to test a proposed new design of turbine which, if successful, will reduce the cost of the main Fundy tidal project by some 10 per cent. However, in my view too much time has already been wasted on studies of tidal power development. While I do not believe it is the final answer to our energy needs, we must utilize every energy source available to us in light of our over-all dwindling oil supplies.
In the past six years, our position has worsened and we are dependent on a few producing countries, not all of them friendly to us for various reasons, and on a thin line of oil tankers stretching half way around the world whose cargoes may not always reach their destination in Canada. This is why I say that Fundy must be developed. In fact, we must look at all possible energy sources. We have plenty of coal in Canada and those responsible for the development of energy self-sufficiency in Nova Scotia have indicated that there is a need for the opening of a new coal mine in Cape Breton.
Until this is done, our economic prosperity is endangered by constantly rising power costs. The opening of a new mine at Donkin is a measure that should be given the highest priority by the federal government, in my view. Even if a new mine were opened today, it would be several years before it operated at capacity. Our premier, the honourable John Buchanan, faces a very difficult problem at present. He is well aware of the need for the opening of a new mine in Cape Breton, and I hope, as I said a moment ago, that this project is given priority treatment by the government.
In addition to this, we must take a new look at the use of wood for the generation of electricity, and must re-examine our peat resources. Peat as a fuel for the thermal generation of electric power is an established energy form. In the Soviet Union, for example, peat-fuelled electric power generation plants have a planned capacity of 6,000 megawatts in 1980. By comparison, 5,225 megawatts of power are generated at Churchill Falls. Canada-this is a fact not generally known- ranks second in the world in terms of peat resources, having well over 23 billion tonnes at 44 per cent moisture, compared to the Soviet Union's 180 billion tonnes.
In the Atlantic region peat, for example in Newfoundland, is quite plentiful. About 17 per cent of the land surface in Newfoundland is composed of peat. The other Atlantic provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, have about 10 per cent of their area in peat resources.
Despite the abundance of this resource, Canada's production of peat for its various uses is very small. In light of the high and increasing cost of oil, interest in peat is increasing, and it is my understanding that Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are undertaking today active peatland inventory programs. These are all forward steps, and I believe it is inevitable that, in the very near future, peat will play an important role in power generation in Atlantic Canada.
We hope that through conservation and the proper use of our coal, as I mentioned a moment ago, of our wood, our tidal power, wind, solar energy, hydroelectric energy and now
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
Canadian propane gas, Nova Scotia will be able to come close to becoming self-sufficient in energy by 1990.
In closing, I commend the Prime Minister and the cabinet for their proposals and I hope that the suggestions I have made will be given fair consideration, with the hope of early implementation of the proposals regarding energy which would be very helpful to Nova Scotia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to address my first few words to the Chair and join all previous speakers in congratulating the Speaker of the House and also the Deputy Speaker on their appointments, which clearly prove the confidence all hon. members have in the quality and the competence of those who were chosen, or rather chosen again, as both held those offices for several years under the previous government.
Secondly, I should like to take this opportunity, after seven years spent in this House, to thank the electors of the riding of Outremont, who for the third time have given me their support in ever increasing majority. Naturally, I take pride in those results which I also accept with considerable humility, for being chosen to represent as large a proportion of the people obviously means added responsibility.
I do rejoice in that support and also noticed, with some measure of humour, on examining the results in my riding that there were nine or ten candidates, unless I am mistaken, going from the Liberal, Progressive Conservative, New Democratic Parties, to Marxist and Leninists of all hues and the Rhinoceros Party. It struck me as quite humorous the day following the election to notice that, in my riding, the Progressive Conservative Party had managed the feat of achieving lower results than the Rhinoceros Party. That, I think, gives a pretty good idea of the popularity of that party in the province of Quebec, and the work that awaits it. That is indeed quite a hurdle to jump.
I should also like to thank the people of Quebec for the support they once again gave the Liberal party in that election.
Not only did Quebeckers give the Liberal party a large majority of seats-indeed the largest number of seats ever obtained in Quebec-they also gave us a record percentage of votes, that is, more than 62 per cent. There is no doubt that this is due in the first place to the outstanding qualifications of our leader, the member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau). This is also undoubtedly due to the devotion and efficient work performed by the Liberal members of Quebec for several years in the House. And I am pleased to note that as a result of the election those Liberal members were reinforced by the addition of a substantial number of new, able, experienced and dynamic members who are joining those who sat during the last session and will make of the Liberal team of Quebec in the
94

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
House a group that will promote the interests of all Quebeckers and also, of course, of all Canadians, since for us there is no contradiction in being both a good Quebecker and a good Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues and the Canadian people, I was eager to hear the first Speech from the Throne made by the first Progressive Conservative government in 16 years. I thought-and I was quite wrong-that my colleagues on the other side had benefited from this long sabbatical period of time spent on the side of the opposition and that they would propose a political and economic program which would ease the difficulties our country is experiencing at the present time, because after a period of reflection that had lasted for over 16 years-in fact, it seems that that is more than enough for any party to prepare itself to govern a country-the people of Canada had a right to expect the Progressive Conservative government to act immediately. They also had a right to expect that action to be coherent and responsible. Coherence and a sense of responsibility, the two things the Speech from the Throne we are discussing today obviously lacks. But could it have been otherwise when we know that the Progressive Conservative Party has badly lacked those two qualities for the past 16 years?
Unfortunately, it was easy to foresee that once in power, this inefficiency, while being its trademark, would nevertheless remain inexcusable in Canada's political and economic context. This Speech from the Throne is nothing more than a bunch of spur-of-the-moment campaign promises. It is nothing more than half-baked policies, clearly unsatisfying for all Canadians, men and women alike. Ultimately, this Speech from the Throne reflects the stubbornness and obscurantism of the Progressive Conservative government in the economic field in general, and in the energy field in particular. As a result, instead of facing a so-called responsible government, Mr. Speaker, I am under the impression, of facing a government that is unable to take decisions, that has lost all sense of its responsibilities, that is juggling with complex problems whose outcome be of vital importance for the country and that makes one contradictory statement after the other, and this has been going on for almost five months now. Let's recall, for example, its decision to move the Canadian embassy in Israel and the disastrous consequences it had for Canada on the domestic as well as on the international front. And all the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) could come up with afterwards was that he had underestimated the extent of the Arab protests. Meanwhile we have lost contracts worth billions of dollars and Canada's name has never fallen into such disrepute as it has in the past few months.
Let us not forget that since the beginning of June this government has governed-and this is a figure of speech of course-in a vacuum, without calling Parliament. In fact, this is the first time in our history that our country was governed without Parliament for so long and it is not surprising that

after such a long delay we should feel disappointed when we read what is referred to as the Speech from the Throne.
Let us see on the other hand what President Carter did meanwhile, last summer for example. After realizing that the energy crisis in the United States was as serious as it was here in Canada, he did not lose five or six months procrastinating and making general statements on this issue. He interrupted his schedule for ten whole days, shut himself up with his advisers in Camp David and then released a specific energy statement to the American people. And this was done last summer, at the beginning of August.
Meanwhile, our government again vainly tried to review fully the question, met in Ottawa, in Jasper, at Lake Mousseau and here and there in Canada, met with the provinces, we are told, yet no conclusion has been reached after all those months in a field which is crucial indeed. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I have to note that in politics ridicule is not a terminal disease because those across the way would be a very sick bunch indeed.
I would like most of all to deal with the energy question, specially with Petro-Canada. The Speech from the Throne remains oddly silent on the energy question, whereas the government itself had recognized that this would be the major issue which the House would face from now until Chrismas. The throne speech contains merely one paragraph dealing with energy where they keep on uttering the same platitudes we have heard since early June. Yet, we would have expected the government to take this opportunity to state exactly its intentions. But in fact, although the name Petro-Canada is nowhere to be seen in the throne speech, it has to be noted that it is hinted at here and there in the speech where there is mention of Crown corporations and their sale to the private sector.
The Conservative government's resolve, its determination to destroy at all costs, Canada's major oil company, has no solid nor reasonable ground. Arguments such as "make room for free enterprise" or "government has no business in that field" are false arguments in the case of Petro-Canada, because, first of all, they fail to take into account past experience in the field of energy and, in particular, of oil. Second, they underestimate the specifics of the present energy situation both in Canada and abroad. Third, if the government is successful in achieving its objectives in this regard, it will be bringing Canada back on the road to foreign dependence.
Let us take the private enterprise argument. There is no lack of private concerns in the oil industry in Canada. That sector even boasts over 700 private businesses involved in oil. There is no lack. What is also interesting to note is that they are not all small and weak. If one looks at the 500 biggest companies in Canada for 1978, one realizes that among the top ones there is a whole series of oil companies: Imperial Oil, fourth, Shell Canada, tenth, Gulf Canada, twelfth, Texaco Canada, twenty-first, BP Canada, fifty-first, and so on.
October 11, 1979

What is aiso interesting to note, on the other hand, is that in this area, if you look at all the companies I mentioned, this is a sector which is mostly, excessively under foreign control. All the companies I mentioned are American or European multinationals which control the oil market in Canada. In fact, those companies have assets and sales of billions of dollars and indeed together as foreign companies control 91 per cent of assets and 95 per cent of sales in the oil industry in Canada.
In light of that, the existence, the complete continuation and expansion of Petro-Canada are essential to this country if we no longer want only to appear to have control over our resources but also really increase Canadian ownership over resources which belong to Canadians in the first place. In suggesting this I am not saying the role of the private sector is not important-as I have already said, there are 700 of them-and I am not saying either that there is no role for foreign businesses; they have made their contribution in the past, they should continue to do so in the future. But in an industry where competition is as doubtful, in an industry where uncertainty and instability are factors we must continually be taking into account, in an industry where any increase in our dependence on OPEC countries and multinationals will only make the situation worse that it is primarily important that Canadians have, particularly in the oil industry, an effective and disinterested tool-and that tool is Petro-Canada.
In that respect, the operations of Petro-Canada since its creation by the former majority Liberal government is more than adequate evidence of the increase of Canadian participation in the oil industry. We have only to look at the latest annual report of this corporation to realize it.
In 1978, Petro-Canada took part in the drilling of 16 of the 26 wells drilled in the most isolated parts of Canada. Off the shore of Nova Scotia, it took part in the drilling of five wells, and under its own initiative or through its interest in Panarctic Oils Limited it took part in the drilling in eight of the ten wells drilled in the Arctic islands. Finally, in western Canada, Petro-Canda drilled 44 exploration wells.
Petro-Canada also places great importance on the development of our enormous tar sand and heavy oil reserves, and thus it is involved in various projects including that of Syncrude in western Canada. Also, agreements have been reached with Saskatchewan Oil and Gas and Gulf Canada, and there has been an agreement with the government of Saskatchewan concerning projects for the exploration, the development and the accelerated recovery of heavy oil in Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, how can a government which claims to be responsible deliberately put an end to all this? Who, for instance, successfully carried out exploration operations in the area of Sable Island after Mobil Oil and Gulf gave up? It was Petro-Canada. Who took up the challenge of prospecting in the most hostile and hardest to reach regions of Canada? Petro-Canada. On whom can the government depend to estimate available reserves and gather the information it requires
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
in the energy field? Petro-Canada. Who, at the height of the Iranian crisis, when Imperial Oil and Exxon were diverting each day to the United States 20,000 barrels of oil from Venezuela which were supposed to come to us, negotiated an agreement with Mexico? The Canadian government, with Petro-Canada.
While wanting to abolish Petro-Canada, the Prime Minister and the minister of energy (Mr. Hnatyshyn) have told us that their ultimate objective was Canadian independence in the field of energy by 1990. Well, this is what they have been telling us since May 22 and even before, but we are still waiting for their plan, that famous plan, and the specifics on how they are going to do it.
I have before me the figures published by the National Energy Board, which is not supposed to be a partisan body, of course. These figures show that in 1978 imported 192,000 barrels of crude a day, net imports after exports, after deducting our foreign sales. The board forecast that we will have to import 826,000 barrels of crude a day in 1990, and 905,000 barrels a day in 1995. As I say, this government is either having delusions when they speak of self-sufficiency within 11 years, or peculiar arithmetic, and I must say, unfortunately, that I often think they have both.
Mr. Speaker, we may believe that if the present course is maintained by the majority of industrialized nations, the oil producing countries will soon demand interstate, intergovernment negotiations. I was pleased to note this very day that the president of Petro-Canada had this to say before the Empire Club in Toronto, and I quote:
The sitution is no longer one in which private oil interests can be expected to always obtain and deliver oil. Each transaction directly or indirectly involves a government presence. Not one drop of oil moves today from the Middle East without a government agreeing to it, and almost every sizeable oil importing nation has its government in the act.
[ Translation]
Who then will be representing the Canadian government if Petro-Canada no longer exists as a true oil company? During the crisis in Iran, when the price of oil on the free markets was reaching disproportionate figures between S30 and $40 a barrel, Walter J. Levi, a leading American expert, an economist of repute, a consultant to both governments and private corporations, was interviewed on the program "Meet the Press" over the NBC network early in 1979. He said:

To avert international crisis, governments will have to step in and recognize that big oil companies and free enterprise programs are just nonsense and would not work.

This is in agreement with the remarks made recently by a Canadian, an expert of repute in Canada, a man with a long

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
experience in energy matters, Mr. Bruce Wilson, who indicated in the Toronto Star, and I quote:

It should be apparent to the new government, which now has the responsibility for ensuring the viability of Canada as a nation and for protecting the interests of the citizens as a whole, that the primary objective of the private sector resource-exploiting industries to maximize profits is incompatible with the need to provide assured supplies of energy for the engines of the economy at reasonable prices.
A decision by the federal government to emasculate Petro-Canada, solely on the basis that it was an election promise, does not give one confidence in the quality or objectivity of the new administration. Rather than disposing of Petro-Canada, the government should be developing comprehensive energy policies and plans designed to head off the bleak future now confronting the nation in the energy field. A much stronger, rather than weaker, federal presence is required.
And I say "amen" to that.

And above all we should not believe that, however the emasculation of Petro-Canada might be achieved eventually, no great harm will be done. Indeed, if the government stands by the public statement made in early September, we would be left only with a skeleton firm, emasculated of its most essential functions and whose profits would not allow it to expand, indeed to continue its exploration and development efforts.
The net result of that absurd proposal will be that we will have two Canadian firms of medium size. One will be nonviable, unable to serve the true interests of Canadian society, and every year it will come and bow before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) to get the money it will need, while the other firm will be viable and will be owned by a number of shareholders who will of course be more concerned with profits and dividends than with the security of our supplies.
Indeed, even the Conservative government of Ontario rejects the approach adopted by the present Progressive Conservative government in Ottawa. I am referring to the paper entitled "Energy Security for the Eighties: a Policy for Ontario". Here is what the government of Ontario had to say in that regard:
Petro-Canada supplements the job being done by the private sector and takes appropriate risks where the private sector is reluctant. Petro-Canada provides Canadians with a better insight into the complexity of finding and developing new oil and gas reserves. Petro-Canada can and should, along with the private petroleum industry, play a leadership role in achieving crude oil self-sufficiency for Canada by 1995. This is the conclusion: Ontario urges the federal government not to reprivatize Petro-Canada but to retain essential functions within a national petroleum company.
Premier Davis is not the only premier with that view. It is shared by a lot of other premiers. It is shared by the premier of British Columbia who, on a CBC radio interview on September 16, said quite clearly that in his view it would be wrong for the Government of Canada to try to follow with Petro-Canada the approach that he had followed with British Columbia Resources Investment Corporation. That is the view of the premier of British Columbia himself, and he had very, very

good reasons which anybody could understand to justify that distinction and that argument.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from a tour in western Canada where I met representatives of and spokesmen for the oil industry. I was surprised to see the large number not only of ordinary citizens but also of spokesmen for that industry who say, "Now, listen. Petro-Canada is there. We are accustomed to live with it so why touch it? Let Petro-Canada live and work with us; we can work closely with Petro-Canada which, as a Canadian corporation, has been of much service to us even if at the start we had some doubts about its usefulness."
And this view is shared by a great many citizens. I urge all my colleagues opposite to read their correspondence and they will see to what extent Canadians are preoccupied by the whimsical policy of the present government. They should read the results of a Gallup poll that have been published today, a poll made throughtout Canada. Its obvious conclusion is that Canadians are for maintaining Petro-Canada. Seventy five per cent of Canadians want Petro-Canada to continue its operations in the prospecting field. And 57 per cent believe that Petro-Canada should pursue its purchasing activities on the international level, and 54 per cent say that Petro-Canada should be involved in retail sales. Those who think otherwise represent only 7 per cent, 18 per cent and 20 per cent respectively. For a government that pretends to be listening and consulting the people, I must say that I never saw a government as deaf as the one before us.

This government has at least one member from Imperial Oil, and a national director of the Conservative party from Imperial Oil, and assistants in ministers' offices from Imperial Oil, but 1 cannot imagine the members on the other side perceiving themselves as being also members for Imperial Oil. This is a view in which they are completely isolated, isolated from the view of the vast majority of the population. I urge this government, if it believes what it has been preaching, to reconsider its approach and its policy and realize that Canada needs Petro-Canada more now than it needed it in 1975 when it was created.
1 would like to say a few words about our motion and the amendment put forward by the NDP. I think that our motion yesterday put the situation and our stand quite clearly and quite adequately when we suggested that the address be amended by adding the following words:
-and this House condemns the attempt of the government to undermine Petro-Canada and supports the maintenance and expansion of our national petroleum corporation, as the property of all Canadians, as the largest Canadian-owned corporation in the petroleum industry and as a major instrument of Canadian energy policy.
The NDP in their amendment stated:
-and this House calls in particular for the corporation to be designated as the sole importer of off-shore oil, and for the corporation to open retail outlets to serve the people of Canada from coast to coast.
October 11, 1979

When we set up Petro-Canada in 1975 we gave it very wide-ranging powers, and we were right in doing so. Petro-Canada is engaged in all aspects of the oil industry since its creation, through acquisition in particular of ARCO and Pacific Petroleums. It is interesting to see that the retail sales of Pacific Petroleums have increased since the acquisition by Petro-Canada, proportionately more than all of their other competitors. I think that it says something, and that is that the public feel that they would like to support an integrated Canadian oil company.
While in Calgary recently I was flabbergasted to meet the president of a Canadian oil company who informed me that he had now switched to Pacific Petroleums for purchasing the gas for his own car and that he was not buying it any longer from other companies. We are not objecting to Petro-Canada having retail outlets. It is within its powers. The question that arises is whether or not this would be the wisest investment for the company to make at the present time.
I do not think that anybody would argue very strongly that we are short of service stations at the present time and that we need to build more service stations. If Petro-Canada has $1 billion to invest perhaps it should be invested in exploration and development of the resource rather than into adding to the number of service stations, or purchasing existing service stations. Be that as it may, that power is in the act, and Petro-Canada is in a position to take the appropriate decision as to the wisdom of undertaking such a development in due time.
The area in which I question the amendment proposed by the NDP is the proposal to designate Petro-Canada as the sole importer of offshore oil. This question was extensively debated last spring when we put forward the Energy Supplies Emergency Act, 1979. That same proposal came from the NDP at that time. The House debated it for several days and rejected it by a margin of 190 to 13. I believe that there were very good reasons for the proposal being rejected. We do not need a monopoly on the foreign supply of oil. It is essential that Petro-Canada be there and that there is an agency to deal with countries that want to deal with a state agency. But it need not be the exclusive purchaser of oil in all countries, however. Canada is better served if there are several sources rather than a single one. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this line should be maintained.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and also offer my congratulations to you, sir, on your reappointment to the Chair. In the last
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
Parliament you had the respect of all hon. members and I am quite sure you will be taking your two new assistants, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) and the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott) under your wing to make them as efficient as you have been over the years.
We have seen a great start to the debate on the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker. There have been a lot of wild statements and charges this afternoon, but very few facts. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) said that the government will do away with CMHC. I should like him to present some evidence of that, Mr. Speaker. This government will do no such thing, as we believe CMHC has provided excellent service over the years. It will remain intact.
If some hon. members wonder which party introduced the first unemployment insurance plan in this country I am delighted to inform them that it was a Conservative government in 1935. There was some delay in implementing the plan because of a Liberal filibuster but it eventually went through. This government is interested in the unemployed, Mr. Speaker.
I should also like to speak briefly about the mortgage interest deductibility plan, Mr. Speaker. There has been a lot of negative criticism of the plan, especially from the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry who apparently is the housing critic for the official opposition. This policy was introduced by the Progressive Conservatives in 1965, Mr. Speaker, so it was not something dreamed up in the middle of the last election campaign as was the New Democratic Party plan. The Liberals now claim to be concerned about homeowners and renters, but I would point out that they had 17 years in which to introduce a mortgage interest deductibility plan that would do something for the country. Of course they did nothing. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) while in opposition made a major announcement on this subject on September 21, 1978. If the Liberals are so interested in housing and renters they should have introduced their own policy at that time. If a bill had been presented to the House the legislation would be in place by now.
The present economic conditions in the country will present certain difficulties in the implementation of this policy, but it is going to be done, Mr. Speaker. I should like to allay the fears of some hon. members and the Canadian public regarding the program, Mr. Speaker. There have been some wild charges to the effect that renters will not receive any benefit, but I would point out that in the last few years there have been considerable benefits for renters due to the action of the provinces and cities.
For many Canadians renting is viewed as a temporary state of affairs until they can afford to purchase housing. According to a recent survey 90 per cent of young Canadians want to own their own homes. The initiative of this government will make it easier for them to achieve that goal. The Liberals had 17 years in which to make that dream come true but they did nothing about it. They have developed a great interest in it now, however, since we have introduced the plan. As mortgage interest and property taxes are a deductible business expense for landlords, renters are receiving similar benefits already. In

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
some provinces rents have been kept down through means of rent control but very little has been done to make home ownership more affordable.
The plan has some spin-off benefit for renters. As more Canadians, encouraged by the Progressive Conservative tax credits, move into their own homes, more rental accommodation will become available, thus taking pressure off those who chose to continue to rent.
It is impossible to meet the needs of all Canadians with one government program. The old age pension, for example, does nothing for the young, while the child tax credit does nothing for people who do not have children. If it becomes necessary to provide subsidies to renters, this will be done through other means, such as shelter allowances.
The federal government is already involved with provincial governments in the delivery of subsidized housing for low income families and senior citizens through the non-profit housing assistance program, the co-operative housing program, graduated payment mortgages for landlords, and other CMHC programs.
This program is being financed by passing the benefits of the government's restraint program on to Canadians. Renters are not being asked to pay higher taxes to assist homeowners.
It would have been much easier to implement the program in 1965 when this party first introduced it, or even in 1978 when it was again introduced by this party.
At the present time the province of Manitoba, recognizing that rising rents coupled with fixed incomes put terror into the hearts of senior citizens, has wisely designed a rent subsidy program to help 9,000 elderly people. This will cost the relatively low sum of $3.5 million. The province of Ontario has allotted additional moneys to assist senior citizens who are renters or home owners.
We could do a lot more for renters and homeowners and indeed everybody else were it not for the totally irresponsible actions of the previous so-called government over the last 17 years, and particularly the last 11 years. Anyone who wants to challenge that statement should read some of the reports of past Auditors General and also the report of the Lambert commission. The Liberal government was spending $1 billion per month more than was collected in revenue yet Liberals have the audacity to criticize this government and offer advice. With their record they should not even open their mouths.

It could have been expected that something would have been done to correct the situation after one of those bad reports, but the situation continued year after year. Things did not get better; they got worse. The Lambert commission brought in 151 recommendations in an effort to clear up the mess created by 17 years of liberalism, and stated that Parliament must insist upon full government accounting. That is something this government can promise, Mr. Speaker. The Liberals did not believe in being accountable to the people.

One reason that we cannot do more for renters and home owners is that the interest charges alone on the irresponsible borrowings made by this so-called government that has been replaced, cost taxpayers $23 million per day. This government, of course, now has to pay those bills. That is not an excuse; it is a fact. The bills have to be paid and that is why we cannot give more for everybody. We are stuck with paying Liberal bills.
This government will implement the report of the Lambert commission and bring back control over expenditures. This all came about because the Liberal government changed the rules in 1968 and 1969. The Auditor General has stated he can only account for half the $50 billion budget and that he does not know where that $25 billion is going. A government which has created a situation like that does not need to offer adivce or criticism. They had 17 years to perform miracles, to help everybody out and to get oil and all the rest of it.
We have heard a lot of criticism about health care, and accusations that the Conservative party is opposed to it. That is an out and out lie, Mr. Speaker. It was this party that introduced health care to Canada. The terms of reference were laid out in 1961 by the Diefenbaker government. All the recommendations contained in the Hall commission report at that time were implemented and, as a result, first class health care was introduced in Canada. A Conservative government introduced all these health care plans in conjunction with the provinces. All the terms of reference are here. All were investigated and the recommendations were implemented.
I was happy to read what the current health minister said to the provincial health ministers. He said, "I have been casting about, in my own mind, for the most appropriate person to conduct such a review into health care to make sure these standards are going to be maintained." He stated, "We are extremely fortunate, I think, that the originator of the Hall commission report, Chief Justice Emmett Hall of Saskatchewan, has indicated to me a willingness to take on this job." I understand Mr. Hall will once again review health care in Canada and make any recommendations that are required.
Our health minister has stated that he is proposing to create a national health care institute of Canada. He has already sent a note to the health ministers concerning such an institute, and additional copies of his note will be passed out. We are very much interested in health care in this country because we are the political party that introduced it in the first place.
The New Democrats and the Liberals in Manitoba have spent considerable time attacking the Manitoba government with regard to health care in that province. I want to read this into the record to give an example of what the provinces are doing under difficult times. Health expenditures in Manitoba have risen from $459 million in 1976-1977, to $503 million in 1977-1978, to $525 million last year, and to $570 million this year. There are not the cutbacks that the NDP and the Liberals are raving about, Mr. Speaker. One-third of the provincial budget in Manitoba is spent on health care.
October 11, 1979

1 would like to point out the percentage of increase for health care in Manitoba. Hospital insurance and medicare payments in Saskatchewan are budgeted to increase this year by 4.8 per cent and 8.3 per cent, whereas in Manitoba they are rising by 10 per cent and 8 per cent. Health care will deteriorate in Saskatchewan if that is only the percentage increase they are giving to their hospitals and to the rest of their health care plans. I hope Mr. Justice Hall will start in a province governed by the NDP where they have serious problems.
In the last federal election we were treated to some of the most irresponsible statements I have listened to by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) over national television. He was on TV just about every second night saying that doctors are opting out only in provinces where there are Conservative governments. He left out the province of Saskatchewan which has an NDP government. There are three different schemes in Saskatchewan under which doctors can opt out, and they have allowed doctors to opt out for the last 16 or 17 years. So the NDP says, "We don't like opting out in Conservative provinces but it is all right if the NDP government of Saskatchewan allows opting out." That is an example of irresponsible statements that we get from the NDP, completely misleading the Canadian people.
The NDP got quite a bit of support in the last federal election. They picked up a few seats. But a lot of Canadians have been wondering what on earth they did voting for that party, after hearing statements by a former president of the NDP in Manitoba, Mr. Frank Syms. I have known Frank Syms for many years. He is a harmless little socialist. He has run many times for the NDP unsuccessfully, but finally he has seen the light. Mr. Syms quit the NDP because of a "Commie" takeover.
I will read a report from the Winnipeg Tribune. The article reads, "Long-time NDP member J. Frank Syms has turned in his party card in protest against what he describes as a takeover of the NDP party by apologists for communism and communists." How do you like that? Mr Syms says in the article, "There are too many high profile New Democrats who find nothing good in our system but who entertain no criticism of communism. Over the past five and more years, I have watched with concern and opposed the takeover of the Manitoba NDP machinery by a coalition of militant, radical groups and individuals. They include the more militant of the Status of Women advocates, anarchists, Revolutionary Workers, Party adherents, sympathizers and Trotskyists" and on and on.

speechtext:
Those are words from a member of the NDP party for many years, who was a past president of the NDP in Manitoba. He was an NDP appointee, being the head of the liquor board for eight years.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry has stated in the House today with regard to deteriorating health care in Manitoba, that its social programs are declining. Obviously he is not acquainted with the facts, and apparently has no intention of getting the facts. I have an example of what one
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
province is doing, and I am sure the others are doing the same thing.
In Manitoba a $138 million program has been undertaken to renovate the health sciences centre. That is a lot of money for a province the size of Manitoba. Breast cancer victims are now eligible for rebates on breast prostheses. Major financial assistance is now available to families purchasing hearing aids for children under 18. A $4 million expansion to the Manitoba Cancer Treatment and Research Centre has been completed. An expanded dialysis unit costing $583,000 has been opened at the health sciences centre. The government has assisted in expansion of the open heart surgery unit at St. Boniface Hospital. Construction of the $32 million Seven Oaks hospital is nearing completion. We did not stop that. It was started by the NDP administration, which is fine. We could have stopped it but we didn't. Extensive fire safety upgrading has been undertaken at a number of Manitoba hospitals and personal care homes. Since 1977 $36.4 million has been committed to provide 1,291 personal care beds, and $10 million of this figure has come from the private sector. Seventy-five per cent of pensioner home owners have been provided with full school tax relief.
On and on it goes, and yet these people have the audacity to stand up in this House and say we are against senior citizens and against people who are sick. One-third of the budget is being spent on health care, and as you can see by the items I have just put on the record they are completely misleading the Canadian people when they stand up in this chamber and make ridiculous statements.
The NDP and the Liberals have used this chamber to attack the Manitoba government on other issues. This practice was started in the last Parliament. In Manitoba most of the federal election was spent on debating policies of the provincial government. The NDP did not have any of its own so it started attacking the present Conservative administration with a lot of false information. The economy was a popular subject. In the last two years under the Conservative government, 11,000 new jobs have been created. This is nearly triple the rate of the NDP. All of these jobs have been in the private sector and do not represent a burden on the taxpayer.
Another interesting announcement was made last week by a minister in the Manitoba government that four of the government Crown corporations that they had sold to the private sector are all thriving and have all hired more employees. They are doing a great job now that the government has its sticky fingers out of it. This past summer 8,631 summer jobs were created for students by private industry. In 1978 private capital investment, the real generator of jobs, increased by 22 per cent. Manufacturing investment is going up by 34 per cent in 1979, double the national rate. Yet members opposite say the economy is terrible there. Commercial building permits in the city of Winnipeg in 1978 increased 3,800 per cent. That is an indication that things are going very well. Just imagine if the NDP came back in. That sends shivers up and down my spine. In the last Parliament I read many statistics into the record which I obtained from financial institutions which were

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
assisting businesses in moving out of Manitoba when the NDP was in power there. The loss was staggering. The amount of money leaving and the number of jobs lost were staggering.
Manitoba has the third lowest unemployment rate in Canada. Exploration spending in the mining and the oil industries has almost doubled. Mining exploration under the NDP in Manitoba came almost to a grinding halt with the minister they had in charge of northern development and mining.
Leadership has been shown in Manitoba. Hydro rates have been frozen for a period of five years in order to assist the people of Manitoba. Since July, 1979, Manitobans have enjoyed the third highest minimum wage in Canada. The eight years the NDP were in power in Manitoba were disastrous for us. It was a very costly experiment. We saw the NDP in the Chinese food business. I like Chinese food, but I certainly do not want to buy it from any NDP government. That went bankrupt. Then they got into the aeroplane manufacturing business. The last thing in the world a provincial government should get itself involved in is manufacturing aeroplanes. Another $40 million to $50 million was lost by the people of Manitoba. On and on it goes.
I want to get back to health care for a moment. Not all members of the NDP are irresponsible. I have here a statement by a former NDP leader, Mr. Tommy Douglas. He was referring to the Hall report back in the 1960s. He said it was one of the finest reports ever written on the subject. He credited Mr. Diefenbaker and his Conservative government with laying the foundation stone for medicare. I think Mr. Douglas should be given credit for recognizing that fact. I do not expect that he would be going around the country making such irresponsible statements as those made by his NDP colleagues. According to them, our party is against medicare, hospitals, senior citizens, and all that irresponsible nonsense.
I do not know what kind of constructive criticism we will be receiving from the Liberal party, now that it is in opposition. Liberals seem constantly to be squabbling about leadership. There are many newspaper articles being released by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). He came here in 1972, the same time I did. He writes letters stating that he wants his leader replaced, or that he has some other complaint about his party. I have never heard him say anything good about his party. I do not know why he wants to stay in the Liberal party when he has so many complaints about the way its members conduct themselves. He is concerned about Liberal caucus members who have been given specific responsibilities. The hon. member for Vaudreuil complains that his colleagues are making public policy statements without any discussion in caucus. The Liberal party is very disjointed. There are articles: "Trudeau under attack", "Disgruntled Liberals urge end to former PM's reign". They are certainly having their problems over there.
I would like to speak briefly about Petro-Canada. I do not know what everybody is getting all excited about. Petro-Canada has certainly become a very emotional issue. The

Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has stated that we are going to be keeping many parts of Petro-Canada. He has stated that the negotiation of state to state contracts for the importation of crude oil, where necessary, will be looked after by us. He has stated that there will be promotion of exploration in frontier areas with increased Canadian participation and at a pace which cannot be expected of the private sector alone. We will work with them.
I was in Calgary recently at a Canada-U.S. parliamentary meeting. We met with Petro-Canada officials there. They showed us films of some of their developments which are being undertaken in conjunction with the private sector. We have no objection to that at all. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has stated that promotion, along with frontier exploration, of tar sands and heavy oils research and development will be done by Petro-Canada. I do not know what the Liberal energy critic is getting so excited about. Those are things he is concerned about, and we are not going to abandon them.
The energy critic pointed out that there are 700 oil companies in Canada. I do not know how many oil companies we need, but that seems to be an awful number of oil companies; plus we have Petro-Canada. I am sure the task force, when it turns in its report later on this month, will be making its recommendations. Whether we implement them or not I cannot say right now, and neither can the government. We have to wait until the task force files its report.
I would like to give hon. members an idea of the size of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Perhaps there are a number of branches of that department in existence which could perform the same functions Petro-Canada performs. There are over 300 branches, divisions and agencies employing some 4,000 people. Just look at the government telephone directory-11 pages! What are they all doing? Perhaps they could be performing many of the functions of Petro-Canada. 1 think we must look carefully at duplication. We are taking a responsible position. There is nothing wrong with reviewing a federal government department or agency. There are 400 others which we have to review to find out what they are doing. They will have to justify their existence.
We are acting in a responsible manner in reviewing all these various government departments. We are not just going to close our eyes and let them operate on their own. We do not know whether they are operating efficiently, or whether they are required, or anything else. We have a responsibility to Canadian taxpayers to find out if all these 400 Crown corporations and the hundreds of divisions and branches in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources are required. We are taking a responsible position. Because we do that we will be criticized. We should be praised for checking to see if taxpayers' money is being spent properly. I do not see anything wrong with doing that, but that is the kind of thing that we get from the Liberals and the NDP.
The Conservative party was interested in energy long before the Liberal party even thought of it. I remember when the roads to resources program was introduced in the fifties by the
October 11, 1979

Diefenbaker government. That was ridiculed by the Liberals. Canada would be well on the road to being self-sufficient today if that program had been carried on when the Liberals came back to office in 1963, but they disbanded it and made a lot of smart aleck remarks about our building roads from igloo to igloo, and that sort of thing.
I would like to quote from a speech made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), who has been involved in energy for many years in this country and who worked with our former leader, Mr. Diefenbaker, with respect to the roads to resources program. He spoke at the opening of the Dempster highway, which was delayed for about seven or eight years by the Liberals. He said:
Actually, the Dempster highway was one of the main anchors of the whole concept of the roads to resources program. If one looks at a map of Canada on a conic projection, it will be seen that Canada from Labrador to Yukon is a part of a circle of land that centres on the Arctic Islands.
These islands were once part of the tropics of the earth. From Stefansson's time, the eyes of the world's explorers were focused on this potential treasure house of resources. Stefansson named several of the islands after ministers of the cabinet that sponsored his explorations. This angered Mackenzie King who proceeded to name an island after himself.
That is typical. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain also stated:
When I became minister in 1957, I immediately tried to pull all the information together on how we could get a road through to the Arctic coast as fast as possible. From my analysis of the Patey report of 1952, based on U.S.A. resources, I knew that Canada should have access to Arctic Islands hydrocarbons by 1980.
This was back in 1957. Just imagine what would have been the result of continuing that program.
We are very concerned about energy. Energy has been a priority of the Conservative party for many years. The hon. member went on to say that when he became a minister he found a map by some unknown civil servant in the old department of the interior which projected generalized routes to the Arctic. He added:
I found oil and gas regulations which gave everything to the finder. The regulations were obsolete. The department had no real resource people left in it so I went to resource people in industry. Dr. Link, Dr. Sproule and my brother, all of whom had then retired, and they assisted in the roads to resources program.
I just want to make it clear that we are the party which has shown leadership over the years in introducing the unemployment insurance plan and mortgage deductibility. We introduced the roads to resources program years ago, and these constant references to us by Liberals and spokesmen for the NDP as a party not conscious of people's needs are entirely unfounded. Mr. Speaker, we are more conscious of people's needs in this country than the NDP and Liberal parties put together. Back in 1973, even in opposition we were pursuing a natural resource policy for Canada. I have in my hand a number of documents we put out in 1973 with regard to oil supplies and all the rest.
I hope this will straighten out the position to some extent, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for your indulgence.

I am somewhat reassured during the first three days of the sitting of this, the Thirty-first Parliament, because 1 believe that once the news of the weather in Ottawa this week reaches Cape Breton I may be unopposed in the next federal election.
With reference to the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) said yesterday that Canadians should raise their expectations. From what we have heard since May 22 the only Canadians with any expectations are those who form the present government. Certainly we in Atlantic Canada cannot have any expectations as long as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) is running loose. Prior to May 22 certain areas in Atlantic Canada were promised assistance in the form of the decentralization of various government departments. But following the May 22 election the President of the Treasury Board decreed that this should not take place and the excuse he gave was that the government had to save money, but that money should be saved only in some of these constituencies.
In Nova Scotia decentralization plans were cancelled only in two constituencies represented in this Parliament by opposition members. This is more than just a coincidence when one considers that there are only three constituencies in Nova Scotia represented by opposition members and that decentralization plans had not been made for the third constituency.
In Cape Breton-The Sydneys decentralization was to take the form of almost 400 jobs for the area. Land was purchased and the architectural work for a new building was well under way. There is no question but that in addition to providing jobs decentralization would have revitalized the downtown area of Sydney, from which there would have been a spin-off effect evident in new stores and buildings.
1 feel the fact that the government has broken most of the promises it made during the election campaign-and kept the ones it should have broken-is unacceptable to the people of Canada. It is certainly even less acceptable to break the promises of the previous government. The actions of the President of the Treasury Board amount to nothing more than petulant vindictiveness and I appeal to the hon. gentleman to reconsider his action of cancelling decentralization in the
102

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. MacLellan
Sydney and Antigonish areas. Decentralization planned for Sydney has an importance to that region which far outweighs the cost involved.
The Cape Breton economy cannot withstand the cancellation of these decentralization plans. The latest figures given by the department of development in Nova Scotia showed an unemployment rate of 17.4 per cent in industrial Cape Breton. We are not asking for charity but merely seek an early investment by the Government of Canada in the future of our area. We have no doubt that if our economy follows the course it should take, our economy will be viable in the future. However, we are presently trying to keep our communities intact until such time as the modernization of Sydney Steel, the opening of new coal mines and a more enlightened approach by Canadian National Railways and CN Marine put the Cape Breton economy in a positive position.
With respect to Sydney Steel Corporation, the situation is serious. The British North America Committee has stated that the cost of producing basic products is increasing at three times the rate of inflation and if governments such as ours fail to take positive action there will be a shortage of these basic products by the end of the twentieth century. One of these basic products is steel. Despite this very sobering information, the government has chosen to do nothing to aid Sydney Steel Corporation financially. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacKay), who during the last Parliament was very vocal in trying to right the wrongs of this country, is suddenly very quiet. I guess he has found that things are very different when you get on the other side of the investigation.
The minister responsible for DREE has promised that substantial aid will be forthcoming. He has not said how much, or when, but he has gained the faith of the people of Cape Breton. Steel workers and merchants alike genuinely believe the minister when he says substantial aid for Sydney Steel is forthcoming. Let us mark this moment, Mr. Speaker. Let us hope that the minister, who in the past has been so much on the side of the individual, will keep his word to the people of Cape Breton who have placed their faith in him. Of course he will need to obtain money, and this brings us back to the President of the Treasury Board. I say to him that Sydney Steel can be profitable and urge him to have some faith in the people of Cape Breton.
It would seem that the government is fast becoming elitist and the Speech from the Throne reflects this. However, I do take some heart from the comment that the government will build upon the strength of the regions. Sydney Steel is a strength in eastern Canada, and if the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion or the President of the Treasury Board has any doubts on this question, I would be very glad to inform them of why this is so. In fact I have been trying for over three months to see the Minister of DREE, and now I think he is in danger of giving me an appointment for next week, for which I am very grateful.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take this opportunity of joining in this debate on the motion in reply to that very excellent and welcome throne speech His Excellency the Governor General delivered earlier this week. It was a throne speech unlike many others I have
The Address-Mr. Andre
heard in that it was devoid of a lot of what one columnist called purple prose. It was in fact a terse description of the plans and programs of this government for the coming legislative term.
Some members on the opposition benches have decried the fact that there was nothing new in the throne speech. Several members of the media have said there were no surprises. It was not intended that there should be any surprises. We campaigned earlier this year outlining the programs, policies, and activities or actions we would implement as a government, and the people of Canada by their vote approved of that program. We are now carrying forward our promise to implement it.
The government has clearly indicated it intends to fulfil its commitment to reduce government involvement in the lives of individual Canadians, and its involvement in the economy. We intend to reduce the profligate and wildly extravagant spending patterns that have become the norm in Canada. We intend to reduce the $12 billion deficit, and balance the budget. We do not intend to continue the practices of the previous government of saddling future generations with our extravagances.
The government intends to reduce the involvement of government in the lives of Canadians in other areas. It is the government's intention to reduce its involvement by regulation, and thereby reduce the burden that imposes. We intend to reduce these involvements that result when we have a government, as we have had in the past, which assumes it knows what is best for Canadians, and knows better than the individual what is right, what is proper, and what will lead to a great future. We recognize and have confidence in the ability of Canadians as individuals. We recognize that it is the Canadian citizen, the Canadian individual who is most important, and that if we look after the interests of the Canadian citizen the country's interest will be looked after very well indeed.
That was the thrust of the throne speech. It was not intended to be surprising, but to contain those things we committed ourselves to a long time ago. There was nothing secret. We explained our programs to the people of Canada, they cast their ballots, and now we are going to follow through with those commitments.
