speechtext:
After the privilege of serving in this House for five years, Mr. Speaker, obviously I cannot come here at this time and pretend to make my maiden speech. But even after some 200 interventions during the last Parliament I am still in a sense making my maiden speech this evening since 1 now represent the newly named area of Crowfoot rather than Battle River.
I should like to take a few minutes to reflect on my constituency, something I did not do the first time I took part in debate in this House. I do so because this will provide a nice lead to a concern I should like to share with the Parliament of Canada this evening.
Chief Crowfoot was one of Canada's great men. He took a group of people through that very devastating period from 1860 to 1870, a period during which the Indians of the prairies lost everything they depended upon for their livelihood. They lost their source of energy, their source of food, their source of housing, and their ability to maintain a certain lifestyle. All this disappeared with the disappearance of the buffalo. Chief Crowfoot saw the obligation of leading his people through that tragic and devasting period.
It was during that period of time that Chief Crowfoot lost his entire family to smallpox. He was cited by the first prime minister of this country for his tremendous nobility, wisdom, and vision of the future. Chief Crowfoot rebelled against Sitting Bull in Montana and refused to fight with him in Canada. He resisted the Crees and opposed them during the Riel rebellion. Chief Crowfoot has left his mark on early western Canadian history through his fine ability to lead, to speak, and to make his point.
Let me quote directly from what Chief Crowfoot said at the time of the signing of Treaty 7. At that time, an aging man, he said, "In a little while I will be going from amongst you. Where I have come from and where 1 shall go, I do not know. What is life? It is like the flash of the firefly in the night, it is like the breath of the buffalo in the wintertime, it is like the little shadow that races across the grass and loses itself in the sunset." A person who would say those lines is obviously a man

of the land, and it is to that subject that I wish to address myself tonight.
We have heard with just cause concerns tonight and in previous days about energy. We cannot diminish the fact that there is an energy problem, but I submit that the energy crisis in this country as painted by many is so minuscule, so infinitely small in proportion to another greater problem to which Canadians must very quickly address their attention, and that is the rapid disappearance of our agricultural lands.
Four-fifths of the world's population suffer from malnutrition. Approximately 12,000 children a day under the age of 5 are dying from starvation, and some 70 million human beings suffer permanent and irreversible brain damage every year from the lack of protein. In terms of a world perspective there is no crisis so important as that of retaining our source of food production.
The fact of the matter is that there are only two sources of food. One is soil and the other is water. Our water is basically established. Fisheries supplies will increase and decrease in accordance with their management. But the fact about our soil is that we are not making it any more. There are of course some exceptions, and I will come to those a little later in my address.
Half of the agricultural lands of Ontario are now permanently gone, and they are not coming back. There are a great number of acres of additional Ontario land that is tremendously threatened. I come from the province of Alberta. It is a fairly large province, not the largest in Canada but it would encompass most of the countries of Europe. While we are looked upon as a province that has traditionally had agriculture as its number one industry, the truth of the matter is that of the seven classes of soil, our province has only one per cent of class one agricultural soil.
There are some very interesting and important facts that we should recognize. One is the agricultural pattern of how our country was established. Three members of my party and three members of the official opposition party last November had the privilege to join in some good friendship and in some sincere hard work. We had the occasion to visit in the Middle East. While we were there I noted the rich fertile valleys of Egypt and some other Middle Eastern countries, and to see the villages on the rocky hilltops and the larger cities on the tops of mounds amid the rocks. The first thought I had was of the great wisdom of the forefathers of those countries who decided to build their cities there. But it did not have to do with wisdom at all in the sense of agricultural lands. It had to do with the fact that culturally they defended from the top of the mount down. It was easier to shoot a bow and arrow and a cannonball down than it was to shoot upward.
Likewise, here in Canada, we established this country basically on the principles of agrarian society. The old pioneers who came west knew something about fertility. They knew that the deep, rich, black soil was where the poplar trees grew tall and straight. So it is not without coincidence that the cities
October 11, 1979

of Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Regina, Lethbridge, Red Deer, Edmonton and Grande Prairie are all built in the middle of old geological lake beds of silted out soil, the best of our agricultural lands. Of the cities of the prairies that I have just mentioned, I have included every one of the important cities except for Calgary and Medicine Hat. That brings us to the very serious fact of agricultural land uses.
Of our class one and two soil, 50 per cent of all that remains in Canada today is within 35 miles of our largest 22 cities. When we take a look at the program and planning of urban acreage sprawls across the country, we can see that we are facing a crisis situation of paramount importance because our agricultural lands are decreasing at a rate that is far, far too rapid.
Let me put this into perspective. In the world today there is one acre of agricultural land for every citizen on earth. In Canada there are three acres of agricultural land for every Canadian. By the year 2005, if we make no change in our agricultural land policies in this country, we will have three quarters of an acre of agricultural land for every Canadian. As I began my talk about agricultural land tonight, I mentioned that there were some 12,000 children a day under the age of five dying of starvation. That is yesterday, 12,000; today 12,000; tomorrow, another 12,000; and by the year 2005 without any jurisprudent change in the direction that we are going, we will have less agricultural land in Canada than the present world average for world citizens. That is totally and absolutely unacceptable.
I have raised this concern because I see in my own province the city of Edmonton, a fine and a beautiful city, now making application to expand its boundaries by some six times its present size. That cannot go unchallenged. More important, when I mentioned earlier tonight that the cities of Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Lethbridge, Red Deer, Edmonton and Grande Prairie were all built in the middle of old geological lake beds, the fact of the matter is that every one of those cities has all kinds of ample room to expand without going on to agricultural lands, except for the city of Regina. I submit that it is not a question of whether we have acreages nor a question of whether or not we have lawns. Canada does not have to live in concrete towers. We have the second largest land mass in the world. The problem is that there is only 7.5 per cent to 8 per cent of our land in the class one and class two soil zones in climatically favourable areas.
That means that we have to begin to pick and choose where we put our transport systems, and where we put our cities. We have to put a priority on food production in the recognition that today when we eat a meal 40 per cent of what we pay for came from some other country. We think of Canada as a country that is rich and able to produce and export food because we sell a great deal of wheat and we have a red meat market that exports from the country.
But we also depend very heavily on green vegetables and fruits which come from elsewhere. When we consider the simple fact that 40 per cent of what we pay goes somewhere else, then this soil is not something to be wasted. Unfortunate-
The Address-Mr. Malone
ly I will have to pass by this subject without dealing with it in the kind of detail that I would like tonight because I do not have my notes with me.
1 want to share with the House what some other countries are going through today because of the realization of what the land is worth. In Holland, 21 per cent of the whole country is recaptured land. They are now building a dike that will take
1,600,000	acres of land from the North Sea, but it will be 11 years before it comes into full agricultural production. Many people in Holland live in boat houses on the canals because the land is too precious to use for building.
Throughout Peru, throughout Asia and much of India, the mountains have been terraced up one side and down the other, the steps honed by human beings with shovels. Much of the soil is infertile; it contains no nitrogen, no phosphorus, no potassium. They start from bedrock and build animal dung and fibre up to the surface in order to develop the land. Throughout much of the subcontinent enormous draining programs are being established in order to try to recapture that little bit of the vital element that produces food, namely, soil.
We in Canada have grown up thinking that soil is dirt, not recognizing that all through the history of mankind every advanced culture has started from the foundation of a ready supply of food and a cheap source of energy. The sources of energy were not always oil and gas, or an adequate coal or wood supply. In the Greek or Roman period the energy source was mainly the slave trade. That is not a condition that any of us in the House today would endorse, but nevertheless they had cheap energy. Interestingly, an analysis of the history of cultures that failed shows that everyone of them fell as a result of war or the loss of their food rather than lack of an energy source.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that we have no energy crisis; we have a systems crisis. We have all the pulp we need to make energy from wood; we have the sun, we have the wind, we have nuclear. Like it or not, it is there; we may not want to use it but that is a decision for Parliament to make. There are an infinite number of ways in which we can develop energy. What we need, Mr. Speaker, are the systems. There is no infinite way to develop a food capacity, however, if we destroy one of the two things that produce food.
I submit an activity like the plan of the city of Edmonton to expand its boundaries is not something about which we can say, "Shame on you; you should not be doing that." No mayor is going to ask the people to re-elect him saying, "Look what I have done. I stopped all the growth in this city. Because I stopped the growth I have saved agricultural land; therefore, you should re-elect me." That is not going to happen and no one can blame city fathers for wanting their cities to grow.
If we are to take a responsible attitude toward agricultural land use, then policies must be developed by one of the two upper levels of government in this country.

That means that the provinces and the federal government ought to play a more significant role than they have in the past. In this chamber we must realize that resources are obviously a provincial right. Because I believe that agricultural land use is such a very important long-term issue, I would encourage this House to do what it can to persuade the provinces to co-ordinate and concentrate their efforts on something that is going to be vital for our children, our grandchildren and, indeed, our great grandchildren. It is of paramount importance that we do not continue to let other countries with less developed resources than ours, spend virtually all their human energy in the search for some adequate form of food production such as moving back dikes into oceans, or carving away at mountains, while in this country we use some of the best soil in the world as backfill for basements.
As 1 said earlier, Mr. Speaker, all the aforementioned cities on the prairies, except Regina, have alternatives from which to choose. The city of Edmonton wants to expand its boundaries and, as I said, we cannot blame them for that. Fortunately, however, a move of about 15 or 20 miles to the northeast of Edmonton opens into a large area of solonetzic soil which could easily accommodate a city of vast size.
We have an obligation to get the message out clearly, to get it out often, and to never cease realizing that soil is something we cannot waste today and make again tomorrow-that it is somehow like energy, and when the oil is gone, we can use coal, and when the coal is gone, we can use nuclear. We cannot eat coal and we cannot eat nuclear and we cannot eat sunrays, Mr. Speaker. We need food, and food comes from soil or from water.
We hear of young people in the farming communities of this country who want to go into farming. Sometimes when they are asked what their plans are they reply, "I am going to be just a farmer." Mr. Speaker, farming is the business of food production, the most important business in the world. No society ever advanced that did not have that as its first industry either through the ready production of food within the society itself or very ready access to food purchased fom neighbouring societies.
We in this House must recognize this as a matter of immense, long-term consequence. We must view it in the perspective of the ancient societies where land ran out. In the districts of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers of the Middle East people did what most other cultures of that time did when their food ran out-they moved somewhere else. That is basically what has happened in modern societies; when we ran out of food we moved to a new, fertile land to find a food supply. Then, Mr. Speaker, some fool found that the world was round, and now that we have occupied it all, there ain't no more. This is all we have and it is limited.
I want to conclude by saying that in representing the constituency of Crowfoot I am following a man who as an Indian leader of the prairies recognized very clearly the importance of food, the importance of nature and of living in harmony with it. I would hope that we can somehow imprint upon the minds of parliamentarians and of all Canadians that

we must give much greater recognition to the one sure thing we know about soil: they are not making it any more and, by golly, we need it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate and thank the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. We must admit that it is not easy to shed some of the apprehensions we feel when we stand and speak in the House. We all feel a little nervous. Now that I have congratulated them, I should like to tell these hon. members that tradition compels us to be extremely polite with those who make their maiden speeches in the House and that we will tend to be less and less polite as time goes by.
I should like also to congratulate you and your colleagues on your appointments Mr. Speaker, and wish you the best of luck during this Parliament where debates will no doubt be dramatic at times. Finally and more especially, I would like to say how much I am grateful to my constituents of Ottawa-Vanier who were kind enough to re-elect me as their member. It is an honour which I accept in ail humility and, in addition to expressing my thanks, I can assure them that I will try to fill that important position by using my few qualifications with the appropriate dignity.
The part of a member, Mr. Speaker, as we know quite well, is to serve as an intermediary between the individual and the government machinery, that enormous and anonymous institution managing public affairs. Each of us tries to follow and understand the problems and decisions which directly affect him while that enormous anonymous machinery takes decisions for us. In addition to the many requests which they receive, members of parliament write to ministers and officials to obtain information that they will pass on to their constituents. This means that while they listen carefully to get acquainted with the views of their constituents, they must also try to think it over before taking a position which will be that of most of their constituents.
As a member of Parliament, all matters of concern to Canadians concern me. But, Mr. Speaker, my first duty lies with the concerns of my electors of Ottawa-Vanier. I love all Canadians, but I also love dearly the electors of Ottawa-Vanier, and I shall allow myself a few comments on my riding.
The city of Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, and the national capital region have become economically dependent because it is the seat of the federal government. It is quite natural that the main industry of the capital of a country should be the government of that country. However, to ensure economic stability, and bearing in mind the impact on the local economy of the measures announced by the present government, we will
October 11, 1979

have to seek and find, here in the area, a greater economic stability based on a policy of diversification and growth, in order for the city to have fewer of the characteristics of a one-company town or more of the several-companies town. The cities of Ottawa and Vanier must in the future take fuller advantage of the facilities found in the area. The national capital area must in the future make better use of the natural resources and its partly developed possibilities. There is need for closer co-operation between the numerous municipalities, the various levels of government in the area; the aim should be to draw them all together.
In Ottawa-Vanier, the sustained revival of the lower town area, the city of Vanier and other sectors of downtown Ottawa, will make of it an important centre of attraction for the area. The development of Rideau Centre-God knows it has been discussed in this House-will encourage promoters and small business whether it be restaurants, theatres, both cinema and legitimate, or boutiques. It is a healthy thing for downtown Ottawa to have a shopping centre as a counterpart of the shopping centres which in the last few years have multiplied in suburban areas. City cores should perhaps be given new life in order for our large centres to offer spots where life is worth living. We are also all aware of the fact that the city of Ottawa and the surrounding area are dominated by a private sector which is oriented towards services, many of which are related to the federal government. There is no doubt that if the federal government wants to reduce the number of civil servants- which is the present policy of this government-more entre-prises will disappear or run into financial difficulties. So it is very urgent to take measures to alleviate that dependence on the federal government and to endeavour to find other economic generators.
The national capital area offers tremendous opportunities. It can become a research and development centre of first importance. The Government of Canada and the universities in this area-we have two-do a lot of research, especially in agriculture, natural sciences or communication techniques. The activities of the federal government and those institutions of higher learning give Ottawa and the surrounding area the opportunity to attract a private sector in research and development in an area which can hardly be compared with other areas in the country. So we must attempt to diversify, while attracting new industries to Ottawa and the national capital region.
That is why any proposal aimed at growth and diversification opens promising perspectives. The surest way to growth is the development of existing opportunities, and I am not going to speak of all opportunities, because I would not finish tonight. I am thinking of tourism, light industry, small factories, and the like. Mr. Speaker, there is enough potential here to give our region the economic vigour it once had. These ideas, Mr. Speaker, could easily be pursued or implemented through planning and co-operation procedures, action which
The Address-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier would involve the private sector, the regional government, the regional municipalities and the National Capital Commission. Meetings to this end have already been held. One in particular was held last August with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) at which time a resolution was passed to have the President of the Treasury Board set up a panel of experts to study the impact of government decisions on the stability of the local economy. The President of the Treasury Board promised to set up this panel before the end of September. Nothing has yet been done, or at least nothing has been said publicly which would show that he has kept his promise. Since he is made to bear the responsibility for public service cutbacks, one is led to believe that he either is not as interested as he should be in this region or else he does not live up to his word. We shall see!

I would like now to turn my attention to other matters dealing with what the Conservative party has led us to believe is their social policy. As Liberals, we on this side are dedicated to the individual. Our dedication to the individual extends to just and equitable treatment of all individual Canadians in matters of human rights and social policy. Pensions, unemployment insurance, universal health insurance coverage, and housing are examples of social policies which respond to the needs of individual Canadians. The government, on the other hand, has spouted only rhetoric about its commitment to equitable social policy.
One minister of the Crown has stated that the government will remove the universality inherent in the national pension scheme. Another minister talks about reforming unemployment insurance and, in doing so, he has advocated drastic cuts which would affect expectant mothers, single individuals, and Canadians in economically underdeveloped regions. Still another minister of the Crown has advocated and implemented measures which will give tax credits to home owners while totally and unforgivably forgetting the poor and those who rent. The government's professed commitment to the individual must be qualified. The government is committed only to some things for some Canadians.
Already the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) has redefined the criteria for the Canada Works program to exclude a number of legitimate potential participants in my riding. Under the Liberal government my riding was eligible under the Canada Works program because the labour surplus rate was in excess of 7 per cent. High unemployment was concentrated in small areas of my riding, especially in lower town and Vanier. Today, because of redistribution, several thousand constituents have been added, and my riding became ineligible under the Canada Works program. There are just as many unemployed as there were before. There are just as many unemployed individuals who have not changed except that they have now become statistics. Because of the increased number of people in the riding they have lost

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier
their importance under the Canada Works program and are not eligible for any more grants.
The government says it is currently undertaking a review of the unemployment insurance program. The government's lack of concern for individuals in this domain has been striking, as if somehow they did not count as unemployed. They have been denied eligibility for unemployment insurance. Unattached individuals will be penalized because they are unattached. It does not seem to matter very much that statistics show that unattached individuals are in fact the very people who are in need of unemployment insurance.
The average family income in Canada last year was $20,101, while the average individual was earning somewhat less than $8,254 annually. Is the government aware of the number of working women between 55 and 65 who would suddenly be ineligible for unemployment insurance? How many of our youth will be told that they might as well move back home because now they are ineligible for unemployment insurance even though they have made determined but unsuccessful efforts to find or create employment for themselves? The government will have to answer all these questions in the months to come.
We welcome the measure mentioned in the Speech from the Throne which commits the government to a review of retirement policies and pensions for the aged. We hope, however, that the government will not introduce new measures which would in any way tamper with the universality of the Canada Pension Plan. Madame Pelletier in my riding of Ottawa-Vani-er should in no way be penalized because she and her departed husband had the foresight to provide for retirement. There will be no justice for Canadians in any such scheme which removes universality.
I would like to speak briefly about the measures the government has announced to allow mortgage interest tax credits for homeowners. While it is to be applauded that some taxpayers are getting a break, the government can only be condemned for its failure to provide similar breaks for other Canadians. The government gives some money to a select few, and pays for it by taking it away from all of us. The vast majority of constituents in my riding are renters. Are they to be penalized because they are too poor, or because they rent, or because they have decided not to own homes? One hon. member on this side pointed out yesterday that since high interest rates have come in with this government, the $1,500 tax credit on mortgage interest has been completely offset by higher mortgage interest. Young Canadians will have no home at all to look to in the future with such contradictory policies.
My point has not been to criticize the government unduly or unfairly. The government speaks consistently of wanting to cater to the individual and to allow the individual to grow and to prosper. I suggest that the abandonment of a social policy designed to provide a respectable standard of living to those who cannot provide for themselves would be an inequitable and unconscionable act.
As Liberal critic on Treasury Board and on personnel matters as they relate to public servants, I would like to

comment now on some of the directions the government has taken. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and his colleagues are trying once again to give the impression to Canadians-and it is the wrong impression-that the rapid growth of the federal public service is something which has got out of control. The fact is that from 1968 to 1978 the federal public service, including Crown corporations, grew at an average yearly rate of 3.1 per cent, in response to demands from a growing economy. In the same period the Canadian economy grew at an average annual rate of 4.4 per cent, after subtracting the effects of inflation. In other words, the federal public service grew less rapidly than the economy.
The Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board are trying to hide from the public the fact that the real growth in bureaucracies has been in provincial and municipal governments. Even before the last election the growth of the federal public service had been reduced to zero. Contrast that with Alberta, where the provincial public service grew on an average by 7.4 per cent a year from 1974 to 1977, and in Saskatchewan by 6 per cent. Municipal bureaucracies in Alberta grew by 5.7 per cent yearly during the same period, and in Saskatchewan they grew by 7.3 per cent. The record, of course, is held by a fellow by the name of Levesque, who sponsored a growth of 13.5 per cent in Quebec's public service in the first year of his administration.
Neither the Prime Minister nor his hatchet man, the President of the Treasury Board, have made it clear yet how reductions in the federal public service can control the growth of these other bureaucracies. Indeed, with their disposition to give away federal responsibilities they may only be adding to these already large bureaucracies. Is this new government trying to make the federal public service pay for the sins of other governments?

speechtext: Or the previous government?

During the recent campaign we were assured that reductions would be made by selling off Crown corporations and by attrition. How will the government avoid lay-offs when it has implemented a blanket cutback of 2 per cent? We are told in press reports that next year it will be 10 per cent, so evidently people will be directly affected, laid off and looking for work.
On the subject of attrition, in recent times Manitoba, which has one of the only governments which has succeeded to some extent in cutting back on public servants, did it, but it maintained-and I think it was right-that it should never use attrition as a way of reducing its public service. The hints and leaks in recent times about major cutbacks in federal programs and personnel suggest that this new government may be preparing to abandon attrition. With 2 per cent cuts, 10 per cent cuts and all kinds of special interest groups, the word 'attrition" will be redefined. It doen't mean attrition any more. Mr. Speaker. They have redefined the word "attrition".
I wouldn't be surprised to hear the President of the Treasury Board get up some day and say, "Well, we've abandoned that policy, just as we have abandoned other things such as lower
October 11, 1979

interest rates, the embassy move, parliamentary secretaries who were not going to be named-what's another promise here or there?"
It has become increasingly clear that the new government has a very low opinion of its own public service. One of the joys of their rigid ideology is that they need not allow facts to stand in the way of their prejudices. Never mind the opinions of well-informed people across the world who think Canada has one of the best public services there is. Public servants in Canada, in my experience, discharge their responsibilities with the greatest of efficiency. 1 must admit, though, that having read the Lambert commission report I accept most of its recommendations, but if the President of the Treasury Board intends to adopt some of the measures proposed by Mr. Lambert, he must put in hand a policy for the development and training of public servants, especially if he continues to go the route of attrition. I say this because an approach through attrition takes for granted that all positions are equal. But that is not the case.
If you let attrition take its course through the years how can you tell any public servant that he will not be relocated urgently to replace, for example, an inspector on the east coast who has retired, or died, or decided to quit? How does the minister account for the lack of a training or development program, a global approach to look after the staffing of positions which become vacant? I cannot see any logic in the policy of attrition if it is continued without some assurance from the minister, some admission that it does not work and, second, an undertaking that he will try to put forward positive measures of training and developing new talents in the public service.
The government has for several months had its hands on the final report of the Lambert commission on financial management and accountability which was recently made public. It is to be hoped the D'Avignon report on staffing will also become available in the near future. These reports, taken together, might well call for a far-reaching change in the way the public service operates. Can we expect some response from the government to these recommendations in the present session? Or perhaps the government feels the management of the public service is not sufficiently important to merit its attention. We shall see, and we shall constantly remind the government of the importance of review and of putting forward good recommendations to make the public service more efficient and a more efficacious organization.

I should now like, Mr. Speaker, to deal with a question which deserves urgent consideration from a government that would like to be responsible and attentive to the actions of individuals who have at heart the major national objectives.
Yesterday in his speech the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) dealt with an important question, namely, that
The Address-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier Canada means much more than ten provinces, five regions and thousands of municipalities. He said and I quote:
The way to build a whole nation is to realize that Canada is more than the sum of its parts; it is more than just ten provincial feudalities which are warring together; it is more than just a piece of geography. Canada exists if there is a national spirit and a national will.
I shall add that that community of individuals which is Canada must also have a common ideal that reflects the aggregate of the values, brings about satisfaction and gives a meaning to the aspirations of the heart and the mind.

If we read the Speech from the Throne, we find a rather general mention about the various elements constituting our country. I quote:

My ministers believe that the way to build a whole nation is to respect our individual parts, and you will be invited to consider measures to build upon the diverse regional and cultural strengths of Canada.
We may honestly ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, what measures the government will introduce to reach this objective. The laissez-faire attitude of the Prime Minister as concerns linguistic minority groups is certainly more than reason for concern. In a few words, the Prime Minister has often repeated that he would leave to the provinces the full responsibility of rectifying 112 years of indifference and neglect as concerns the development of these communities, whether in the field of education, of health, of justice or of social services. The Prime Minister says, "Let us leave all that to the provinces." Of course, several members on this side of the House must oppose this attitude, and we shall constantly raise the issue of national interest with the Prime Minister to make him understand the importance of the mandate that he has received to speak for all Canadians, wherever they may be and whatever their position. We are all Canadians first, whether our official language is French or English, and our whole nation is based on the fact that most Canadians speak one or the other of these languages. Nearly one million Canadians outside the province of Quebec speak French. Some time I will tell the hon. member how much radiation 1 have had in the last while. If one could witness the growth of technology, its application, its use and its

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Yurko
pervasiveness in the interdependency and interrelationship of individuals, groups, communities and nations in the world itself, one would witness in the unfolding situation the revelation of science to a receptive human mind and the growth and spread of technological application which has accelerated to such vast proportions in the last 50 years or so. Technology has produced serious aberrations in man's own concept of himself and his ultimate destiny and purpose. He has begun to see himself as the ultimate master of his own destiny, as I am sure some socialists have over the last 25 years.
The pervasiveness of technology is so vast and so encompassing that governments at local, intermediate and national levels have increasingly done three things: moved to regulate and control technology, moved to tax the benefits of technology, and moved to redistribute the wealth produced by technology. In doing so governments worldwide have increased all forms of secular authority. In doing so governments and their attendant bureaucracies grew in size explosively and almost irrespective of their political philosophies, whether they be democratic, totalitarian, liberal, conservative, or socialistic in character.
A recent analysis shows the growth of governments in the free nations of the world in the 20-year period from 1955 to 1975. I will not run through all of them, but I should like to refer to a few examples. In the Netherlands the government's share of the gross national product in 20 years grew from 31.5 per cent to 54 per cent; in Sweden from 16.5 per cent to 52 per cent in 20 years; in Ireland from 28 per cent to 50 per cent; in the United Kingdom from 32.5 per cent to 45 per cent; in Germany from 30 per cent to 44 per cent; in Italy from 28 per cent to 43 per cent; in France from 33 per cent to 42 per cent; in Canada from 25 per cent to 40 per cent, now over 42 per cent.

speechtext: What about the United States?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: In the United States it grew from 26 per cent to 36 per cent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about Holland?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I gave the figures for Denmark. In Australia it grew from 22 per cent to 32.5 per cent; in Japan from 17.5 per cent to 25 per cent. This growth in the authority of governments over people's lives has been explosive in just two decades. Indeed a whole new climate of social regulation and cohesiveness developed rapidly. The old authorities of family, community, church and human conscience itself have increasingly been traded and transgressed by the authority of the state. It was and it is a relentless process in virtually all democratic countries. The last 25 years have seen the triumph of de facto socialism and a major concentration of authority over people's lives by governments and their attendant bureaucracies.
It is no wonder that a revulsion has set in throughout many nations as a matter of necessity, indeed as a matter of survival. What is now necessary is more production rather than distribution, more frugalness rather than wastefulness, more initia-

tive and incentive rather than doling out the fruits of technology.
Therefore I agree with the trend in Britain and the statements in the Speech from the Throne. I should like to refer to some of them:
The basic purposes of that change will be to enhance the rights, freedoms and opportunities of individual Canadians-
First, my ministers will reduce the burden of government on the economy by better controlling expenditures.
Second, my government will place greater reliance on individual initiative to generate growth and jobs for Canadians. You will receive proposals for regulatory reform, designed to ensure that the certainty and nature of government regulation encourages individual initiative and planning-
Measures will be placed before you to assist small and medium-size enterprises-
Fifth, my government is committed to making Canada self-sufficient in energy by 1990.
Basically that will be achieved through the private sector. These wonderful statements lead the nation in a direction which is absolutely vital after 25 years of de facto socialism which has encumbered each and every Canadian in this vast country of ours to the extent of literally 45 per cent of the gross national product being directly controlled and spent by governments of this nation.
This brings me to the topic of energy. Let me say first that recently because of technology and its complexities a number of hybrids have evolved linking the public sector with the private sector. I have been responsible for some of these myself. One of the most encouraging directions was the formation of the Alberta Gas Trunk Line in Alberta which has become an enormous success, an efficient and imaginative private enterprise tinged with just a bit of government. Indeed, the Alberta Energy Company is an example of the tying together of private enterprise with a bit of government. It is enormously successful and 1 do not doubt that a few members in this House have a few shares in that company, shares which have gone up quickly from $10 to $40. Indeed, the British Columbia Resources Corporation is another example. There are many examples which have evolved as a result of the power given to a few people through technology. That is what the multinational oil corporations have, a vast pool of technology that gives them access to capital in unlimited proportions enabling them to go anywhere and increase their riches.
Let me say this about Petro-Canada, Mr. Speaker. Petro-Canada as a Crown corporation does not need to be engaged in the operation of service stations, in marketing, in refining, or in LPG plants. Indeed, it does not need to be involved in some of the transportation systems. Petro-Canada can be converted to an instrument of national cohesiveness for the assurance of self-sufficiency in energy in partnership with existing oil companies in Canada, or in partnership, for example, with the provinces, or even through partnership with Canadians, as has been the case with the Alberta Energy Company.
There are a variety of ways that Petro-Canada can be adjusted and tailored to become far more effective in assuring

self-sufficiency in energy down the way than in the manner in which it is structured today. I have had a lot of experience with Crown corporations provincial in scope, and they are not the most responsive type of vehicle for creating wealth.
The industrial world has built a vast productive machine almost totally dependent on what used to be $2 or $1.85 a barrel oil. This made the OPEC cartel not only possible but powerful. That cartel raised world oil prices ten to 12-fold in just six years, and thereby placed in motion an effective system of world wealth redistribution and financial power reallocation. A similar phenomenon is occurring within Canada itself.
Each industrial nation was faced with converting its industrial base from low-cost energy to high-cost energy. During the transition period each nation had to act quickly, and 1 pity the nation that did not or does not move as fast as it should at the earliest opportunity.
Each nation had three choices in adjusting its economy. The first choice was to do nothing and become poorer, with the people of the nation becoming poorer primarily through inflation, which is nothing more than that process which makes all of us poorer whether we like it or not.
The second choice was to live on debt. They could borrow and borrow and borrow, which the United States and Canada have done, to the extent that we have mortgaged our future with the inflation rate now causing considerable hardship in these nations.
The third choice was to produce more. We could produce more, become more competitive in the world economy, competing with some of those nations that are far more productive.
What this government is trying to do is follow that third approach. It is not following the second approach because we have exhausted our ability to live on debt. This nation has mortgaged its future to the extent that the foreign debt, I believe, is no less than $5,000 per capita.
Inflation is no mystery. The United States delayed its inflationary rate by not becoming poorer for a while and now they are suffering a 14 per cent inflation rate. Canada accepted the brunt a few years ago and now suffers a lesser rate of inflation. As I said, inflation is nothing more than a process for making us all poorer. We have been living beyond our means. The resistance to becoming poorer results in a vicious process of government versus government, community versus community, union versus government and management, corporate entity versus corporate entity, and man versus man. The weak suffer the most. Unemployment relegates many to the redundancy heap, and it is perhaps the most vicious way of making people poorer; the aged on fixed incomes, the sick, the weak, those with the least wealth, power and authority; they are the ones who suffer the most. This is the Canadian situation created by the previous government and inherited by the present government. It is not a rosy situation. It is a most difficult situation, Mr. Speaker.
World oil prices will rise. I spent three days in Washington, and every official I talked with there indicated to me the vulnerability of Mid-East oil. Indeed, some pretty serious
The Address-Mr. Yurko
projections of the instability in that part of the world were made behind closed doors. World oil prices will rise to between $30 and $50 per barrel before substitutes for conventional oil become economically feasibile.
The United States has little choice. It has to become involved with substitutes through liquification and gasification of coal, and that nation has something like 24 per cent to 30 per cent of the world's coal reserves. There is that potential there, but what the United States will have to do is convert the entire society which was built on $2 per barrel oil to $30 per barrel oil. This will cause a major upheaval in the United States and I can assure all members in this House that the effects will be felt in this nation in a serious way.
The incentives, indeed the requirements for moving this country toward oil self-sufficiency are therefore paramount. Indeed, it is imperative to reduce our imports. The price of petroleum must rise. Oil pricing is now established by the forces of supply and demand in the world. There is a much greater demand than the present supply can meet. The Iranian situation has proved that. Saudi Arabia has cut back a million barrels a day. This winter will give us another example of the supply not meeting the demand.
Oil is a peculiar commodity. It is very difficult to place a value on it. It was produced by nature over a billion years. Man came along in the last 100 years, dug a hole and took it out of the ground and said it was worth $1.85 a barrel. Who is to say that is right? This is one of the most vitally important commodities the world has ever known. What is its value? Does man produce it? He can produce it from coal and from biomass which indirectly is solar energy, and the costs are in the area of the equivalent of $30 to $50 a barrel. The appetite for oil is insatiable. In the United States alone the consumption tripled in a mere 25 years.
Earlier this year I wrote out the four points of what I thought to be a national energy strategy. Let me just read them for you. The first is security of energy supply to all parts of Canada with the potential for no less than 50 per cent of total energy needs for any region from Canadian sources. The second is Canadian energy self-sufficiency, that is, zero net oil imports, because the nation is self-sufficient in energy today. It is not self-sufficient in oil. It is oil that we import, because we are self-sufficient in energy-self-sufficiency within a maximum period of 15 years or by 1990 if possible from diversified energy sources. Three is a Canadian deliverability of oil and gas to all regions of Canada; oil or gas. Four, maintaining a healthy, competitive and expanding primary and secondary manufacturing industry in Canada through appropriate energy pricing policies. However, it should not be to the extent that productivity decreases and the competitive spirit is killed. There should be a small advantage to Canadian manufacturing, but only a small one to make it efficient and productive, because that is the key behind the revival of the economy.
I also laid out six points forming a national energy plan. In it I included the fact that we need a major thrust in energy

October 11, 1979
The Address-Mr. Evans
conservation through price adjustments and waste use elimination, major new initiatives in increasing conventional energy reserves and supply capabilities including oil, gas, nuclear, hydro, coal, oil sands, heavy oils, enhanced recovery and others.
The third point in my national energy plan was substantive extension of Canada's energy deliverability to and within all regions of Canada; fourth was a program of extensive energy supply and use redeployment on a regional, and use-cost basis. My fifth point was an accelerated program of research, development and the construction of demonstration facilities of new energy forms like gasahol, solar, tidal, wind, biomass and so forth. Finally, my sixth point was a total review and reassessment of present and possible future Canada-U.S. energy intertwinement arrangements. The question which must always be asked is are they always in the Canadian interest?
1 do not know how much time I have left. 1 believe it is very little, but I had hoped to have something to say about the province of Alberta. What does the province of Alberta want? It wants its rights under the constitution. Under those rights it wants to build and to be a dynamic and vibrant part of Canada. It has opened its borders to young men and young women from all across the nation to come and find employment, opportunity, and a future.
In the United States capital and labour move across the face of the land almost unimpeded. In our nation we have a formula process which I support, but it can get out of hand. It is a process called equalization where people are literally forced through economic handouts to stay where they are.
